articles.title: Padres Have Expressed Interest In Tarik Skubal
body: The Padres are among the teams that have shown interest in Tarik Skubal in the early days of the offseason, reports Jon Morosi of The MLB Network. San Diego has been speculated as a dark horse for the two-time Cy Young winner, but this is the first definitive link to the game’s top free agent.

It’s a fascinating offseason for the Friars. They’ve dramatically scaled back free agent spending since the 2023 passing of former owner Peter Seidler. The Seidler family sold the franchise to a group led by José E. Feliciano and Kwanza Jones over the summer. That’s raised optimism among the fanbase about the Padres diving back into the top end of the market.

The Padres’ series of backloaded contracts left them with a dramatically higher luxury tax number than cash payroll in recent years. MLBTR’s Payroll Tracker (courtesy of contributor Ethan Hullihen) shows they finished the 2026 season with a tax number around $269.43MM and an actual payroll in the $224MM range. They’re projected around $193MM in both figures for the 2027 season, including arbitration estimates. Next year’s cutoffs won’t be established until there’s a new collective bargaining agreement in place as MLB pushes for a cap/floor system. (The cap wouldn’t take effect until at least 2028 even if the league were to get the MLBPA to budge on its longstanding firm opposition.)

articles.title: Sal Stewart Wins NL Rookie Of The Year, Earns PPI Pick For Reds
body: The Baseball Writers Association of America announced Monday evening that Reds first baseman Sal Stewart has won the National League Rookie of the Year award. The win earns Cincinnati a pick after the first round of the 2027 draft via the Prospect Promotion Incentive.

Stewart received 20 of 30 first-place votes and was the only player in the NL field to land in the top five on every ballot. He beat out Mets outfielder Carson Benge and Cardinals middle infielder JJ Wetherholt for the honors. Benge received seven first-place votes and was on all but two ballots overall, leading to the runner-up finish. Wetherholt, who finished in third, received the three other first-place votes.

Nolan McLean, TJ Rumfield, and Logan Henderson were the other players to receive one or more votes in the top three. They respectively finished fourth, fifth and sixth in the voting. Bryce Eldridge, Didier Fuentes, and A.J. Ewing were the only other players to appear on ballots (no higher than fifth in their cases).

articles.title: Kevin McGonigle Wins AL Rookie Of The Year, Earns PPI Pick For Tigers
body: The Baseball Writers Association of America announced Monday evening that Tigers infielder Kevin McGonigle has won the AL Rookie of the Year award. McGonigle’s win earns Detroit a pick after the first round of the 2027 draft via the Prospect Promotion Incentive.

McGonigle received 28 of 30 first-place votes. Guardians left-hander Parker Messick earned the other two first-place votes en route to the runner-up finish. Messick is also a top three finisher for the Cy Young award, which means he earned Cleveland a PPI pick in 2027. McGonigle finished second for the two voters who had Messick in the top spot. Messick received 25 second-place votes, placed third on two ballots, and landed fourth for one voter.

Red Sox southpaw Payton Tolle led a crowded field for the third-place finish. Munetaka Murakami, Carter Jensen, Chase DeLauter, Kazuma Okamoto, Tristan Peters, Sam Antonacci, Travis Bazzana, Walbert Ureña, Dylan Beavers and Henry Bolte all appeared in the top five on at least one ballot.

McGonigle’s runaway win doesn’t come as much surprise even in a very strong field. The 22-year-old infielder, who entered the season as the consensus #2 prospect in baseball behind Pittsburgh’s Konnor Griffin, hit the ground running. He had a four-hit performance in his debut and never really looked back. McGonigle batted.278/.376/.430 across 707 plate appearances, entrenching himself in the top third of A.J. Hinch’s lineup by the second week of the season. He walked at an excellent 13.4% clip against a modest 14.1% strikeout rate.

articles.title: Cardinals, JoJo Romero Have Mutual Interest In Reunion
body: 6:17pm: Jeff Jones of The Belleville News-Democrat reports that there’s interest on both sides in a reunion.

11:13am: After shipping him to Milwaukee at the trade deadline, the Cardinals have interest in bringing back left-hander JoJo Romero, reports Derrick Goold of the St. Louis Post-Dispatch. Romero was a crucial cog in a Brewers’ bullpen that dominated en route to a title.

St. Louis closed the 2025 season with an unsettled relief corps after Ryan Helsley and Phil Maton were traded away. Romero filled in at closer at times to close the year and seemed to have a shot to take the job in 2026. Instead, Riley O’Brien emerged as an All-Star stopper. That allowed Romero to stay in his high-leverage lefty role. He racked up 20 holds in 44 appearances.

With free agency looming, the Cardinals sent Romero and Dustin May to the Brewers for outfield prospects Alexander Frias and Josiah Ragsdale. The swap worked out well for both sides. The addition of Romero gave manager Pat Murphy another southpaw alongside Aaron Ashby in the later innings. Romero was scored upon in just one of seven playoff outings. He picked up wins over the Dodgers in Games 2 and 4 of the NLCS.

St. Louis recouped a pair of young outfielders who immediately ranked among their better hitting prospects. MLB Pipeline slotted Frias at No. 5 and Ragsdale at No. 11 in the system. Eric Longenhagen and Brendan Gawlowski of FanGraphs ranked Frias as the third-best prospect moved at the deadline.
[Related: 2026-27 Offseason Outlook — St. Louis Cardinals]

articles.title: Latest On Ben Brown
body: The health of Cubs right-hander Ben Brown is still up in the air. Sahadev Sharma of The Athletic reports that Brown, who battled a neck injury in 2026, still hasn’t been cleared to throw and a future surgery still hasn’t been ruled out.

It’s a frustrating situation for Brown, who appeared to be breaking out this year. He started 2026 in the bullpen but pitched well enough to get a rotation spot by early May. He made his eighth start of the year on June 19. After that, he had thrown 68 innings on the season across those eight starts and his 12 relief appearances. He allowed just 1.88 earned runs per nine.

Brown got a bit of help, as his.243 batting average on balls in play and 79.1% strand rate were both to the fortunate side. But his 24.5% strikeout rate, 7.2% walk rate and 44.6% ground ball rate were all better than league average. ERA estimators like his 2.50 FIP and 3.55 SIERA suggest he would have fared well even with more neutral favor from the baseball gods.

That breakout season was interrupted by the aforementioned neck problems. Brown was placed on the IL June 24, retroactive to June 21, with what was initially described as a neck strain. A few days later, manager Craig Counsell added more info, revealing that Brown had been diagnosed with a stress reaction in his neck. Brown tried ramping up a throwing program in August but experienced a recurrence of symptoms and never made it back to the club.

articles.title: Mets Outright Kyren Paris
body: The Mets have sent infielder Kyren Paris outright to Triple-A Syracuse after he cleared waivers, reports Anthony DiComo of MLB.com. Paris had been designated for assignment last week. This is the first career outright for Paris and he has less than three years of big league service time, so he will have to accept the assignment.

It’s a strange birthday present for Paris, who will turn 25 on Wednesday. The Mets claimed him off waivers from the Angels towards the end of October. Paris has not yet qualified for arbitration. In spite of that, a few days after the waiver claim, the Mets announced that they had signed Paris to a deal for 2027 and then designated him for assignment. The financial details of that contract have not been reported.

It might seem odd for a club to sign a player and then immediately bump him from the roster but it was by design. Teams do this with the hope that the player’s salary is high enough for other clubs to pass on claiming him from waivers, thus allowing him to stick around as non-roster depth. The player, meanwhile, usually gets paid a minor league salary much higher than the minimum for that level.

In this case, it had worked. The Mets can keep Paris without him taking up a spot on the 40-man. He will probably receive a non-roster invite to big league camp in spring training and will try to earn his way back on.

articles.title: Dipoto: Mariners Eyeing Bullpen Upgrades, At Least One Bat
body: With Jason Kanzler installed as the new skipper out in Seattle, the Mariners have one piece of offseason business checked off the list. There will still be a handful of coaching hires to sort out, but with the GM Meetings underway in Las Vegas, the focus will also turn to upgrading roster. President of baseball operations Jerry Dipoto chatted with Teren Kowatsch of Mariners Roundtable following last week’s Kanzler introduction and gave a relatively candid assessment of his group’s targets.

“This year’s bullpen market is pretty appealing,” said Dipoto. “There’s a lot of guys out there we feel like could help us. We’ve already identified who they might be. Whether we can land them or not is a different story. But, we’re looking to add to our bullpen. We’re looking for one, maybe two more bats. And we’d like to add a veteran infield presence. Whether that is part of the bats or just a presence is something entirely different.”

articles.title: Dodgers Claim Christian Cairo
body: The Dodgers announced that they have claimed infielder Christian Cairo off waivers from the Mets. New York designated him for assignment last week. The Dodgers had three vacancies on their 40-man roster and don’t need to make a corresponding move.

The Mets claimed Cairo off waivers from the Phillies in September. He has not yet qualified for arbitration. Regardless, the Mets signed him to a split deal last week and then designated him for assignment later that day. The salary details of the contract have not been publicly reported.

It might seem strange to sign a player and then immediately cut him from the roster but it’s a strategy that has become somewhat common in recent years, with the Orioles being the club most frequently deploying it. The hope is that the player’s salary is high enough that other clubs will pass on putting in a waiver claim. The player will then stick around as non-roster depth. Even if he has the right to elect free agency, the guaranteed money on his deal will hopefully prevent him from doing so.

The best-case scenario for a move like this would be something like Ryan O’Hearn. The O’s sent him through waivers unclaimed in January of 2023. Baltimore got to keep him as depth while using that roster spot to pick up other players. O’Hearn eventually earned his way back onto the roster and was an above-average hitter for the 2023 to 2025 seasons. The O’s traded him and Ramón Laureano to the Padres at the 2025 deadline for six prospects.

articles.title: Latest On Emilio Pagán
body: Right-hander Emilio Pagán recently turned down a $10MM player option with the Reds, thus becoming a free agent. Gordon Wittenmyer of the Cincinnati Enquirer reports that Pagán already has a busy market and would prefer to sign before the lockout, so perhaps he will have a deal in place in the next few weeks.

Pagán turns 36 in May but it’s not surprising that he has a robust market. His 2026 season was okay if you look at the whole thing but he finished on quite a heater. On the whole, he tossed 42 2/3 innings with a 3.38 earned run average. He posted a 6.43 ERA through 14 innings before a hamstring strain put him on the injured list in May. He came off the IL in June and shoved through the rest of the season with a 1.88 ERA in 28 2/3 innings. He struck out 30.4% of opponents and only gave out walks at a 4.5% clip, both excellent figures.

After that showing, Pagán left $10MM on the table in search of more. His earning power is limited by his age but beating that number should be doable. MLBTR predicted Pagán to secure a two-year, $20MM deal this winter.

It wouldn’t be a shock if Pagán’s next deal was with the Reds, as his last two deals were with Cincinnati. Going into the 2024 season, the Reds gave him a two-year, $16MM deal, with the second year being a player option. It was a bit of a surprising pairing, as Pagán’s main issue in his career has been the long ball and Great American Ball Park is fairly hitter-friendly in that regard.

articles.title: Phillies Interested In Ha-Seong Kim
body: The Phillies have some work to do with their infield and are interested in free agent Ha-Seong Kim, reports Jim Salisbury of NBC Sports Philadelphia. Salisbury mentions Mauricio Dubón as another free agent who would fit into Philadelphia’s plans but says Dubón is looking for a multi-year deal. The Phils are targeting a one-year bounceback candidate, making Kim a more likely fit.

There are many moving pieces on the dirt in Philly. In the first months of 2026, the club mostly had Alec Bohm at third base, Trea Turner at shortstop, Bryson Stott at second and Bryce Harper at first. They acquired Luis Arraez at the deadline and shuffled things around because Arraez wanted to stay at the keystone. Stott moved to third, Bohm to first and Harper to right field. But at the end of the season, Arraez, Bohm and utility player Edmundo Sosa all became free agents.

On top of that, Turner’s future is up in the air. He is still under contract but president of baseball operations Dave Dombrowski has said that Turner needs to improve defensively in order to stay at that position. Advanced defensive metrics were not kind to him in 2026. Outs Above Average had him eight below par, Fielding Run Value nine below and Defensive Runs Saved 17 under. The latter number was the worst in the majors for the position. Turner is now 33 years old and will turn 34 in June, so it will be a challenge for him to reverse course with those numbers.

articles.title: Marlins Interested In Adrian Morejon, Alex Vesia, Sean Newcomb
body: A recent report from the Miami Herald’s Barry Jackson indicated that the Marlins were looking for upgrades to the rotation, bullpen, and at least one of the corner infield or outfield situations. Adding some further context, Kevin Barral of Fish On First writes that the team would prefer to bring in a right-handed bat and left-handed pitchers. This makes sense given that the Marlins already have a good number of lefty hitters, and an overload of right-handed pitching. Cade Gibson and prospect Dax Fulton are the only healthy southpaws on the 40-man roster, as Robby Snelling and Andrew Nardi (a non-tender candidate) are recovering from internal brace surgeries.

To this end, Barral lists Adrian Morejon, Alex Vesia, and Sean Newcomb as left-handed bullpen targets on Miami’s wishlist. The trio in general covers a broad range of possibilities for the Marlins’ winter shopping, and while Morejon is in a tier by himself, Barral notes that Vesia is favored over Newcomb.

Morejon landing with the Marlins would count as a big surprise, as it would surely require owner Bruce Sherman to make his biggest free agent expenditure since buying the team over nine years ago. Avisail Garcia’s four-year, $53MM contract represents the biggest free agent deal of the Sherman era. Over the three seasons Peter Bendix has been Miami’s president of baseball operations, Pete Fairbanks’ one-year, $13MM deal from last winter represents the club’s high-water mark in free agent spending.

articles.title: Guardians Sign Antoine Kelly To Minor League Deal
body: The Guardians announced Monday that they’ve signed left-hander Antoine Kelly to a minor league contract and invited him to major league spring training. The Bledsoe Agency client made his big league debut with the Cubs this past season.

Kelly, not to be confused with Pirates left-handed pitching prospect Antwone Kelly, pitched just 1 1/3 innings in his first call the majors. The 26-year-old (27 in December) held the Yankees scoreless in that one-off appearance. Kelly spent the remainder of the 2026 season pitching with the Triple-A affiliates for the Cubs and Dodgers, combining for 50 2/3 innings with a 4.62 ERA, 23.7% strikeout rate and sky-high 16.7% walk rate.

That gives Kelly parts of four seasons at the Triple-A level. He hasn’t fared well there, logging a 5.82 ERA in 120 2/3 innings. Kelly’s 23.5% strikeout rate in that time is respectable, but he’s been his own worst enemy far too often, evidenced by a bloated 16.6% walk rate.

It’s not the most alluring track record, but Kelly is a former second-round pick (No. 65 overall to the Brewers in 2019) who has previously drawn praise for a dominant fastball/slider pairing that could make him an elite reliever if he could even get his command up from its currently dismal levels to merely below-average.

articles.title: Cubs Unlikely To Pursue Tarik Skubal
body: The Cubs have the biggest rotation need of any ostensible contender as we enter the 2026-27 offseason, but having the biggest need apparently doesn’t entail pursuing the biggest name on the market. Sahadev Sharma of The Athletic reports that the Cubs will surely check in but aren’t planning to be real bidders for two-time American League Cy Young Award winner Tarik Skubal.

While Chicago, in theory, should be able to spend with the top teams in the league, that’s never been the playbook for the Ricketts family ownership group. The Cubs have never given out a contract larger than Jason Heyward’s $184MM deal, which is now nearly 11 years old. The team is particularly cautious when it comes to pitching contracts. Jon Lester’s six-year, $155MM deal from the 2014-15 offseason is the largest in franchise history, and Yu Darvish’s six-year, $126MM is the only other $100MM+ contract the Cubs have given to a pitcher.

Skubal, of course, is going to breeze well beyond all of those contracts. It’s all but assumed he’ll break Yoshinobu Yamamoto’s $325MM record for a pitcher — the primary question is one of “by how much” he’ll do so and not one of whether he’ll reach those heights at all.

articles.title: Submit Your Questions For This Week’s Episode Of The MLBTR Podcast
body: On the MLB Trade Rumors podcast, we regularly answer questions from our readers and listeners. With the next episode set for Wednesday, we’re looking for MLBTR’s audience to submit their questions and we’ll pick a few to answer.

The offseason is here. Do you have a question about a team’s approach this winter? A notable free agent? The looming lockout? If you have a question on those topics or anything else baseball-related, we’d love to hear from you! You can email your questions to mlbtrpod@gmail.com.
Also, if you want to hear your voice on the podcast, send us your question in audio form and we might play it. iPhone users can find instructions on how to do so here.
In the meantime, don’t forget to subscribe to the podcast on Spotify and Apple Podcasts.

articles.title: Looking For A Match In A Steven Kwan Trade
body: “As we sit here today, we’re expecting Steven Kwan to be a big part of a contending team next year,” Guardians president of baseball operations Chris Antonetti told reporters during the team’s season wrap-up press conference after the ALCS. This was something less than a confirmation that Kwan will be back with the Guards in 2027, and it could indeed be that Kwan’s “contending team” plays somewhere other than Cleveland.

The Guardians have made a habit of winning without much offense in recent years, and the club’s collective 97 wRC+ (ranking 22nd in baseball) in 2026 was no exception. Trading one of their most dependable hitters therefore doesn’t make too much sense on paper for the Guardians, especially when the outfield in particular has been a weak link, and Kwan adds a ton of defensive value beyond his contributions at the plate.

That said, trading an increasingly expensive veteran a year or two prior to free agency has long been a favored tactic of the Guardians’ front office (not to mention other consistently small-market teams like the Brewers or Rays). Kwan is projected to earn $11.3MM in his final season of arbitration eligibility, before he is slated to hit the open market next winter. Unless Kwan is open to a very team-friendly extension a la Jose Ramirez, chances are Kwan will be playing for another team by 2028 anyway, so trading him now would allow Cleveland to again restock the roster for both 2027 and the future.

articles.title: Tigers Scouted Teruaki Sato, Kaima Taira; Showed Past Interest In Shota Imanaga
body: The Tigers are among the many MLB teams who have scouted Teruaki Sato and Kaima Taira, Evan Petzold reports in a YouTube video exploring several potential targets for the Tigers this winter. Petzold notes Shota Imanaga as a possible rotation addition, with the added detail that Imanaga drew interest from Detroit when the left-hander made his own jump from Japan to the majors during the 2023-24 offseason.

Framber Valdez’s three-year, $115MM contract (which has an opt-out after the 2027 season) is far and away the largest free agent deal the Tigers have completed under president of baseball operations Scott Harris. Detroit’s two-year, $35MM deal with Jack Flaherty from the 2024-25 offseason is second on that list, and while the Tigers have explored larger splurges on such players as Alex Bregman, Harris has been pretty steadfast in his approach of limiting the club’s forays into the open market.

MLB Trade Rumors projects Sato for a five-year, $80MM deal this winter, Taira for a four-year, $72MM deal (with at least one opt-out), and Imanaga for two years and $40MM. Estimates for players coming from NPB to MLB are sometimes particularly difficult to predict, but if these projections hold, Imanaga might be the cleanest financial fit for a Detroit club that is wary of free agent spending. If Imanaga is still on the Tigers’ radar as a potential add as he enters his age-33 season, the Tigers have more data on what to expect based on the southpaw’s three years in the Show.

articles.title: Luis Robert Jr. And The Risk Of Chasing Upside
body: Three years ago, Luis Robert Jr. had just wrapped up quite the breakout season for the White Sox. After showing flashes of his five-tool potential from 2020-22, Robert proceeded to bat.264/.315/.542 with a 129 wRC+ in 145 games for the Pale Hose. He contributed 38 home runs, which still stands a career best, and he also added 20 stolen bases along with +12 Outs Above Average in center field. FanGraphs valued his total contributions at 5.0 wins above replacement.

Robert had signed a six-year, $55MM contract in January 2020, before he’d even debuted in the Majors. The 2023 breakout left the remaining $27.5MM in salary for 2024-25 looking like a bargain. Unfortunately, as is well-known by now, Robert would regress badly at the plate while dealing with significant injuries. A right hip flexor strain limited him to 100 games in 2024. A pair of IL stints for left hamstring strains kept him to 110 games in 2025.

When he was healthy, Robert failed to match the heights he’d set in 2023. In 856 plate appearances from 2024-25, he batted.223 while posting an OPS of just.660 and an 85 wRC+, making him 15% worse than the average hitter. Robert did manage to hit 28 home runs and steal 56 bases in that stretch, but his low contact and on-base percentages kept him from achieving his full potential on the field. The 2025 season brought some improvement in his strikeout and walk numbers, though he was still worth only 1.3 fWAR.

articles.title: Emilio Pagán Keeps Getting It Done
body: Right-handed reliever Emilio Pagán is a free agent after declining his $10MM player option with the Reds. We ranked him at No. 35 on our list of the Top 50 Free Agents, and two of MLBTR’s three full-time writers expect him to rejoin the Reds on a new deal. As noted in that article, Pagán’s extreme fly ball tendencies have made him a curious fit at the hitter-friendly Great American Ball Park, but he somehow keeps getting it done.

Since the 2024 season, 190 pitchers have thrown at least 100 innings out of the bullpen. Pagán carries a 28.4% strikeout rate and 7.4% walk rate in that time, tying the recently retired Kirby Yates for 23rd with a 21.0% K-BB rate. The league average in that three-year span is just under 14%. From a strikeout and walk perspective, Pagán is right there in the second-tier of quality relievers, even though his run prevention numbers keep him from elite status.

The biggest drawback is Pagán’s propensity for giving up home runs. In the last three years, he’s given up 23 homers in 147 1/3 innings (not counting a two-inning opener appearance in 2024). He’s allowed 1.40 home runs per nine innings, ranking 17th-worst in the 190-reliever group. Unsurprisingly, Pagán is also one of the worst in the group at keeping the ball on the ground. Only six relievers on that list have a worse ground ball rate since 2024 than Pagán’s 28.3%. For comparison, the league average ground ball rate in 2026 was 41.6%.

articles.title: Eric Wagaman Elects Free Agency
body: Infielder Eric Wagaman has elected free agency, according to his transactions log at MLB.com. That was the expected outcome after the Mets outrighted him off the 40-man roster a week ago. He’s now on the market as a low-cost, minor league depth option.

Wagaman debuted with the Angels in 2024 and elected free agency at the end of that year following a DFA. He signed with the Marlins for the 2025 season and went on to take 514 plate appearances in 2025, his largest big league sample to date. Unfortunately, Wagaman struggled mightily at the plate en route to replacement-level numbers.

While he struck out less than 20% of the time, Wagaman only batted.250/.296/.378 with an 85 wRC+ for Miami. An above-average 46.5% hard-hit rate was about the only positive on his profile, as his bottom-line numbers lagged far behind the league average output at his primary position of first base. Defensive Runs Saved and other metrics saw Wagaman’s glovework as passable, but he would have had to be a premium defender to make up for the lack of value at the plate. FanGraphs valued Wagaman at -0.4 wins above replacement in 2025.

This year was more of the same. Wagaman posted a 67 wRC+ in just 52 plate appearances with the Mets and played a handful of innings at the infield and outfield corners. He did have a 108 wRC+ for the team’s Triple-A affiliate in Syracuse, though that production came in just 148 plate appearances. Wagaman had struggled badly with the Twins’ top affiliate before the Mets claimed him off waivers at the end of April.

articles.title: “Multiple Teams” Showing Interest In Ty France
body: Coming off an unexpectedly productive season with the Padres, it isn’t a surprise that Ty France is a hot commodity on the free agent market. “Multiple teams are already expressing interest in the 32-year-old France,” The Athletic’s Will Sammon writes, and “the first baseman could find a deal quickly.”

It is fair to assume that France would be open to signing a contract in relatively short order. The lockout will begin once the collective bargaining agreement expires on December 1, adding some urgency to the proceedings for many teams and free agents over the next 24 days. France didn’t sign his last two contracts until February in each of the last two offseasons (joining the Padres in 2026 and the Twins in 2025), so while he is used to long waits, it’s quite another matter to head into the uncertainty of a lockout without a contract already in hand.

The Padres’ minor league deal with France ended up being one of the best value signings of the 2026 season. France made San Diego’s Opening Day roster and never looked back, hitting.295/.363/.502 with 21 homers over an even 500 plate appearances. France’s 141 wRC+, 3.6 fWAR, 47.4% hard-hit ball rate, and 7.4% walk rate were all career highs, and he followed up his AL Gold Glove in 2025 with another excellent defensive performance (+15 Defensive Runs Saved, +7 Outs Above Average) at first base.

articles.title: Ryan O’Hearn’s Adjustments In Pittsburgh
body: The Pirates overhauled their offense last season. Brandon Lowe arrived via trade. Ryan O’Hearn and Marcell Ozuna came aboard through free agency. Konnor Griffin was promoted a week into the season.

The moves came with varying degrees of success, but the end result was an offense that ranked sixth in scoring, sixth in OPS, and ninth in SLG. Those numbers looked a lot better until injuries thinned out the lineup in the summer.

O’Hearn was a key cog in the middle of the order. He signed a modest two-year, $29 million deal after a strong season split between the Orioles and Padres. O’Hearn was an above-average bat for the fourth straight season, finishing with a 109 wRC+. He slashed.265/.330/.440 over 451 plate appearances. A severe quad injury derailed his season in August.

After five unremarkable seasons in Kansas City, O’Hearn broke through as a viable big-league bat in 2023 with Baltimore. He cut down the strikeouts, improved his barrel rate, and hit the ball hard at an elite rate. O’Hearn continued to produce even as he was given more opportunities against same-handed pitching. He settled in as a reliable contributor who didn’t have the typical power of a first baseman/corner outfielder but had a higher batting average ceiling.

The 2026 campaign looked different for O’Hearn. His strikeout rate ticked back up to 22%. He didn’t barrel the ball as frequently, but hit a career-high 18 home runs. O’Hearn hit.265 and posted a.247 expected batting average. It’s not a bad profile, but it wasn’t what we’ve seen in recent seasons.

articles.title: Bryan Abreu’s Place In The Reliever Market
body: The 2026 preseason played out perfectly for Bryan Abreu. Teammate Josh Hader was dealing with a shoulder injury that was going to cost him the first two months of the season. Abreu would have a clear runway as the Astros’ closer, the ideal audition as he neared free agency.

And … he faceplanted. Abreu gave up 13 earned runs over his first 11 appearances and tumbled out of the closer gig before the end of April. He was banished to low-leverage work and didn’t climb back into a late-inning role until it was too late. Hader returned in June and put together a tremendous season.

Abreu had been an elite setup man for the past three seasons. From 2023 through 2025, he ranked second among all pitchers with 87 holds. Only Tyler Rogers had more in that stretch. Abreu led the league with 38 holds in 2024. It was the most for any reliever since Addison Reed put up 40 in 2016.

Houston has always had a trusted closer since Abreu emerged as a big leaguer. Ryan Pressly had a firm hold on the job in 2022 and 2023. The Astros signed Hader in 2024. Abreu has filled in at times, but he’s maxed out at nine saves in a season. He’s never had an extended look as the ninth-inning guy.

articles.title: Red Sox Notes: Front Office, LeVangie, Kelly
body: The Red Sox front office has thinned out in recent seasons. Multiple executives have found bigger roles with other teams. President of baseball operations Craig Breslow has yet to backfill some of those positions, but that could change this offseason.

“It is pretty clear that that executive leadership circle is down not just bodies, but down really talented people,” Breslow told Tim Healey of the Boston Globe. “A nd we’ve got to find the right people to emerge and to put into place there.”

Former assistant general manager Paul Toboni got the top gig with the Nationals last offseason. Boston didn’t make any additions at the time. This winter, it was AGM Taylor Smith heading out the door. Smith took over as the Athletics’ POBO in mid-October.
Breslow said there haven’t been any hires yet, but bringing in reinforcements in the front office is “near or at the top of my list.”

Healey relays that there has been some movement in the ranks after Smith departed. Senior director of baseball analytics Dan Meyer was promoted to vice president of baseball research. Senior director of baseball systems Patrick Coglianese is now vice president of baseball systems.

It’s unclear whether Breslow would hire/promote a direct No. 2 or just expand the present group. Raquel Ferreira, Michael Groopman, and Eddie Romero are currently in AGM roles. Groopman interviewed for the A’s job that ultimately went to Smith.

articles.title: Max Scherzer Shares Offseason Plans
body: Veteran right-hander Max Scherzer isn’t done just yet. The future Hall of Famer will pitch in “lockout games” this offseason to gauge whether he’ll pitch in 2027, he told Jon Heyman of the New York Post.

Scherzer was noncommittal about his future before his final start with the Blue Jays. With his family in attendance, he fired seven innings of one-run ball with seven strikeouts against the Reds. It certainly had the feel of a sendoff performance, with an electric Toronto crowd backing Scherzer throughout the game.

That last outing came on short rest in a meaningless game for the standings. Part of the motivation for Scherzer seemed to be chasing down longtime rival Justin Verlander on the all-time strikeout leaderboard. He came up a bit short, with the seven punchouts getting him to 3,557, three behind Verlander. Moving from ninth to eighth on the list might not be enough to convince a normal player to keep pitching. Scherzer has proved to be a different level of competitor. It’s not out of the question that the idea of catching Verlander pushes him to play next season.

It won’t come as a shock that Scherzer dealt with several health issues in his age-41 season. He missed time with forearm, ankle, and back injuries. Scherzer ended up tossing 84 2/3 innings around the IL stints, nearly identical to his 2025 campaign with the Blue Jays.

articles.title: Blue Jays Re-Sign Lazaro Estrada To Minor League Contract
body: The Blue Jays have re-signed right-hander Lazaro Estrada to a new minor league deal, according to Baseball America’s Matt Eddy. Estrada opted for minor league free agency at season’s end, as he was designated for assignment and then outrighted off Toronto’s 40-man roster back in August, and then never added back to the 40-man.

The 27-year-old Estrada has spent his entire pro career in Toronto’s organization, ever since he first signed with the team out of Cuba in 2018. Estrada’s long stint in the minors finally paid off with two MLB games (7 1/3 IP) in 2025, and then a slightly longer look of 13 innings over eight appearances this year. A right shoulder impingement sent Estrada to the injured list for about two and a half months this season, which extended his stay in the majors for service-time purposes even if he wasn’t able to pitch.

Over his 20 1/3 career frames in the Show, Estrada has a 6.64 ERA, 20.7% strikeout rate, and 12% walk rate. His Triple-A resume consists of a 5.06 ERA, 23.25K%, and 7.88BB% in 133 1/3 innings for Buffalo, with 24 of Estrada’s 44 appearances coming as a starting pitcher.

articles.title: Details On Braves’ Rotation Search
body: The Braves’ rotation overcame several injuries to post very solid numbers for most of the season, though a lack of depth caught up to the team in the playoffs, as Chris Sale and deadline pickup Tyler Mahle were the only pitchers trusted to operate as true starters. With Mahle and Martin Perez now free agents and questions about health and consistency still swirling over several other Atlanta starters, it’s no surprise that the Braves are widely expected to seek out rotation help this winter.

Gabriel Burns of the Atlanta Journal-Constitution looks at the free agent market to see how many starters are plausible fits for the Braves, and adds a couple of interesting details about two potential targets. Nick Pivetta has drawn interest from the team “in [the] past, but there are currently concerns about his elbow,” Burns writes. The club is also wary of Casey Mize’s injury, which is part of the reason Atlanta held off making a full-fledged push for Mize this past summer. As Burns puts it, “t he Braves were prominently linked to Mize at the trade deadline, though that interest was overstated.”

articles.title: Mets Sign Robert Stock To Major League Contract
body: The Mets announced Friday that right-hander Robert Stock has been signed to a one-year, Major League deal. MLB.com’s Anthony DiComo specifies that Stock’s deal is a split contract, so the righty will earn differing salaries based on his time on New York’s active roster or in the minor leagues.

Stock turns 37 later this month, and is a veteran of six MLB seasons. After posting a 4.71 ERA over 55 games and 72 2/3 innings with four big league teams during the 2018-21 seasons, Stock spent the next three seasons pitching in South Korea, Mexico, independent baseball, and with the Brewers’ Triple-A squad. Stock returned to the majors in the form of two appearances and 2/2 innings for the 2025 Red Sox, and last winter signed a minors deal with the Mets.

It seemed like Stock’s 2026 campaign could be over before it even began, as he underwent surgery for thoracic outlet syndrome last March. However, Stock returned to minor league action by mid-June, and was selected to the Mets’ active roster at the beginning of August. Stock started seven of his eight games for New York, and posted a 5.93 ERA, 19.7% strikeout rate, and 10.2% walk rate in 30 1/3 innings of work.

A bout of finger numbness ended Stock’s season in mid-September. While such an issue is certainly troubling for a pitcher with his TOS history, the fact that the Mets have already made a move to re-sign Stock indicates that the club isn’t too concerned about his health. Stock was averaging 95.8mph on his fastball this season, so his heater didn’t appear to be any worse for wear in the wake of his TOS surgery.

articles.title: Nationals, Jacob Young Agree To Extension
body: The Nationals are locking center fielder Jacob Young in as a key part of the roster, as the two parties have reportedly agreed to a four-year, $23MM contract extension. The contract contains a fifth-year option that’s valued at $8MM, and Young would receive a $2MM assignment bonus if the Nats trade him while on this contract. Young, a client of Excel Sports Management, had been arbitration-eligible for the first time this winter. MLBTR contributor Matt Swartz had projected a $2.3MM salary

Young, 27, has been the Nationals’ primary center fielder since 2024. He posted poor offensive numbers in 2024 and particularly in 2025, but was close to league-average at the plate in 2026 (.252/.318/.390). Since establishing himself as a big league regular in’24, Young carries a.248/.311/.340 batting line (82 wRC+).

While the righty-hitting Young doesn’t provide much in the batter’s box, he’s a high-end defender with excellent speed. He’s swiped 66 bags over the past three seasons but hasn’t been overly efficient, as those steals have come in 91 attempts (72.5% success rate). However, Young went 18-for-22 in steals this past season, and the real selling point on his skill set lies in his glove anyhow.

articles.title: Royals, Hobie Harris Agree To Minor League Deal
body: The Royals are in agreement with reliever Hobie Harris on a minor league contract, reports Ari Alexander of Boston 7 News. The Gaeta Sports Management client will be in big league camp as a non-roster invitee.

Harris has spent the last two seasons in the Boston system. He didn’t get a major league opportunity with the Red Sox, instead pitching mostly with Triple-A Worcester. Harris posted a 4.15 ERA in 31 outings with the WooSox in 2025. Harris missed the first half of the’26 season to injury, returning to throw 24 2/3 frames of 2.55 ERA ball down the stretch. He struck out more than a quarter of opponents but walked over 15% of batters faced, which wasn’t enough to get a look in a strong Boston bullpen.

The 33-year-old Harris has 16 games of major league experience, all of which came with the 2023 Nationals. He surrendered 12 runs (11 earned) with more walks than strikeouts across 19 1/3 innings. Harris has a 95 mph fastball but leans more heavily on his splitter and cutter. The University of Pittsburgh product carries a 4.26 ERA across parts of six Triple-A campaigns.

articles.title: Tigers Outright Yilber Díaz
body: The Tigers sent right-hander Yilber Díaz outright to Triple-A Toledo, according to the MLB.com transaction tracker. Detroit designated him for assignment on Monday when they dropped their offseason roster count to 40.

Díaz was claimed off waivers from Arizona in late June. He spent most of the remaining season on optional assignment with Toledo, though he made a couple brief appearances on the big league roster. Díaz pitched four times as a Tiger, allowing four runs across 5 1/3 innings. He’s thrown 37 1/3 big league frames over parts of three seasons, posting a 6.27 earned run average. Díaz has a modest 15.5% strikeout rate against a lofty 11.9% walk percentage at the MLB level.

The Venezuelan-born Díaz was viewed as one of the better starting pitching prospects in a thin Arizona farm system a couple years ago. He has a power arsenal but was held back as a starter by a lack of a viable changeup and subpar command. The D-Backs moved him to the bullpen in 2025. Díaz has posted big strikeout numbers in the minors but still isn’t throwing enough strikes to stick in the majors, even in a middle relief capacity. He worked 54 innings of 3.50 ERA ball with a 28% strikeout rate and an untenable 15% walk percentage in Triple-A this year.

This is the first time that Díaz has cleared waivers in his career. He’ll remain in the Detroit organization and should receive a non-roster invite to Spring Training. Díaz has exhausted his minor league option years, which limits the flexibility to shuffle him back and forth between Triple-A moving forward.

articles.title: Twins Hire José Martínez As Minor League Coach
body: Former MLB outfielder José Martínez is taking a job in the Twins’ system as a minor league hitting coach, he announced. Martínez concluded his playing career in 2025 after a run in the Mexican League and winter ball in his native Venezuela.

Martínez played five seasons in the big leagues. He’s best known for his 2016-19 run with the Cardinals, for whom he had a trio of double digit home run seasons. He split the 2020 season between the Rays and Cubs. He signed with the Mets for the’21 campaign but suffered a meniscus tear during a Spring Training in a collision with an umpire. Martínez missed the season, was dropped from the roster at the end of the year, and never appeared in the majors again.

The right-handed hitter finished his career with a lifetime.289/.356/.447 batting line. He didn’t have a lengthy MLB run but was 18 percentage points better than an average hitter on a rate basis, measure of wRC+. This will be his first coaching stint in affiliated ball.

articles.title: Corbin Carroll Undergoes Elbow Surgery; Expects Mostly Normal Offseason
body: Diamondbacks outfielder Corbin Carroll tells Nick Piecoro of the Arizona Republic that he recently underwent elbow surgery to remove loose bodies from his right elbow. The procedure used the NanoNeedle, the same technology used in Tarik Skubal’s surgery earlier this year. Carroll planned to start swinging in November. That offseason work will now be delayed but only by two weeks.

Carroll tells Piecoro that he felt some discomfort in that right elbow, which is his non-throwing arm, during the season. That discomfort worsened lately, which eventually led to this surgery. The NanoNeedle is a fairly new technology. In essence, it’s smaller than other arthroscopes, which hopefully leads to smaller incision and therefore less pain, swelling and recovery time. In Skubal’s case, it seemed to work, as he returned in about six weeks from a procedure that would usually take a few months.

With Carroll, it should be even less significant. As mentioned, this surgery was performed on his non-throwing arm. Also, position players can usually return from elbow surgeries quicker than pitchers. Carroll’s offseason swinging program was set to start in November but will now be pushed by a few weeks into December. Apart from that, it will hopefully be a normal winter for Carroll.

articles.title: Mariners To Hire Tanner Swanson As Bench Coach
body: The Mariners are hiring Tanner Swanson as their new bench coach, reports Joel Sherman of The New York Post. Swanson had previously been working for the Yankees as major league quality control coach and catching coordinator.

It’s a homecoming for Swanson, who is now 44 years old. He’s a native of Washington state and played college ball for various schools there. He eventually moved into coaching at the high school and college levels. He entered the professional ranks when the Twins hired him as a minor league catching coordinator in 2017. He got his first big league job with the Yankees in November of 2019.

As Sherman points out, Yankee catchers have generally been well regarded in recent years. He points out that current Yankees Austin Wells and J.C. Escarra have strong framing marks while former Yankees such as Kyle Higashioka, Jose Trevino and others have also done well.

Swanson will presumably doing far more than working with catchers in Seattle. A bench coach is generally considered a manager’s second-in-command, so Swanson’s duties could be more diverse with his new club. He will be working under a relatively green manager. The Mariners hired Jason Kanzler this week. In addition to being a first-time skipper, Kanzler is just 36 years old and has a pretty short coaching résumé.

Swanson will try to help Kanzler learn quickly on the job as the Mariners try to bounce back from a disappointing 2026 season. Manny Acta was the bench coach in 2026. He and several other coaches were dismissed in September shortly after the Mariners parted ways with manager Dan Wilson.

articles.title: Zack Kelly Clears Waivers, Will Become Free Agent
body: Red Sox righty Zack Kelly went unclaimed on outright waivers following his recent DFA, reports Chris Cotillo of MassLive.com. He has more than three years of major league service and, as such, can now become a free agent.

Kelly, 32 next March, has a solid big league track record and pitched well in limited action with Boston this season before a fracture in his right elbow ended his season. He tossed 16 1/3 innings and recorded a 3.31 ERA with a 19.7% strikeout rate and 9.9% walk rate. Dating back to his 2022 major league debut, the former undrafted free agent has pitched 131 big league innings with a 4.04 earned run average, a 22.4% strikeout rate, a 10.2% walk rate and a 45.4% ground-ball rate.

Kelly averages about 96 mph on his four-seamer and sinker alike — the latter of which he only began throwing in 2025. He used to rely on a changeup as his go-to secondary pitch, but he’s more recently ramped up the usage of a new 90-91 mph cutter and paired that with an 81 mph slider to round out his repertoire.

It’s not yet clear exactly how long Kelly will be sidelined. His original IL placement came in late July and was first attributed to elbow inflammation, but follow-up testing eventually revealed the fracture. Wherever he signs next, he’ll be controllable for at least three more years if he’s added back to a major league roster. However, he’s also out of minor league options, which means he’ll have to stick in the majors or else be designated for assignment again.

articles.title: Guardians Claim José Tena
body: The Guardians have claimed infielder José Tena off waivers from the Nationals, per a team announcement. He’d been designated for assignment earlier in the week. Tena was originally a Cleveland signee as an amateur out of the Dominican Republic but was traded to the Nats back in the 2024 deadline deal that brought outfielder Lane Thomas to the Guardians.

Now 25 years old, Tena once ranked as one of the top prospects in Cleveland’s system. He sat ninth in their system at MLB.com ahead of the 2022 campaign and 11th at Baseball America’s rankings. He’s a lefty-swinging infielder who’s experienced at every spot on the dirt to the left of first base, though he’s far better suited at second and third than he is at shortstop.

Tena has appeared in parts of four major league seasons between Washington and Cleveland. He’s taken 659 plate appearances in the bigs and turned in a.240/.303/.358 batting line — 17% worse than average, by measure of wRC+.

It’s not an especially encouraging line, particularly when juxtaposed with Tena’s career 27.5% strikeout rate (including a 31.3% mark in a career-high 288 plate appearances this past season). However, he has good bat speed, makes plenty of hard contact and boasts a stout.295/.362/.486 batting line in nearly 700 career plate appearances at the Triple-A level. There’s above-average raw power in Tena’s bat, but his penchant for whiffs has undercut his ability to drive the ball.

articles.title: Nationals Designate Kyle Nicolas For Assignment
body: The Nationals have designated righty Kyle Nicolas for assignment, the team announced Friday. His spot on the 40-man roster goes to newly acquired left-handed reliever Reiver Sanmartin, who just came over in a trade with the Giants.

Nicolas, 27, was acquired from the Orioles in early July after they’d designated him for assignment themselves. He’s pitched a nearly identical number of big league innings (105 1/3) to the man to whom he’s losing his roster spot (105 2/3) but with shakier recent results. Nicolas had a nice showing with the 2024 Pirates, but the former No. 61 overall draft pick (2020) has been rocked for 27 runs in 45 1/3 innings (5.36 ERA) over the past two seasons.

Although Nicolas throws quite hard, sitting better than 97 mph and at times reaching triple digits, he doesn’t miss bats like one would expect for a pitcher with such high-end velocity. He’s fanned only 21.5% of his major league opponents, and most of the whiffs he garnered came in his rookie campaign back in 2023. He’s punched out just 19.6% of his opponents over the past two seasons — and he’s done so while walking a whopping 14.8% of the batters he’s faced.

Nicolas posted a 3.29 ERA and fanned 29.1% of his opponents in 27 1/3 innings with the Nationals’ Triple-A club in Rochester this season. That sounds good until also weighing the jarring 18.7% walk rate he issued. He’s pitched 138 2/3 career innings at the Triple-A level, missing plenty of bats but also doling out free passes at a 16.6% clip.

articles.title: Giants Trade Reiver Sanmartin To Nationals
body: 12:45pm: The two teams have announced the swap.

12:30pm: The Nationals are acquiring left-handed reliever Reiver Sanmartin from the Giants, reports Spencer Nusbaum of The Athletic. Minor league righty Robert Cranz is headed back to San Francisco in return. The Giants designated Sanmartin for assignment earlier in the week.

Sanmartin, 30, pitched 21 1/3 innings with the Giants this past season and logged a 4.22 ERA, 17.2% strikeout rate, 7.5% walk rate and colossal 63.8% ground-ball rate. The 6’1″ southpaw has pitched in parts of five major league seasons — the other four all coming with Cincinnati — and carries a 5.37 ERA in 105 2/3 frames overall.

Sanmartin works primarily off a sinker that sat 91.7 mph this past season. He complements the pitch with a slider and changeup both used about equally (roughly 27% apiece) and a seldom-used four-seamer that checks in about a half-mile north of Sanmartin’s sinker.

In parts of 10 minor league seasons, Sanmartin carries a 3.40 ERA in 564 1/3 innings. That includes a 4.04 mark in 214 Triple-A frames, where he’s fanned a batter per inning (23.6% overall) with very strong command (6.2% walk rate). As one might expect looking at his big league work, Sanmartin has a track record of posting huge ground-ball rates throughout all levels of the minors — including a rate north of 60% across the past three Triple-A campaigns.

articles.title: Hitting Coach Aaron Bates To Leave Dodgers Organization
body: Dodgers hitting coach Aaron Bates is departing the organization, reports MLBTR’s Tim Dierkes. He’d been offered a multi-year contract to stay, but the two parties couldn’t come to terms on a final agreement. Bates’ departure closes a 12-year run with the Dodgers that saw him contribute to World Series titles in 2020, 2024 and 2025.

Bates, 42, had a nine-year playing career, mostly in the minors. He was a third-round pick by the Red Sox back in 2006 and briefly reached the majors in 2009, going 4-for-11 with a walk in what would be the only 12 plate appearances of his MLB career. He spent a couple years in the Twins’ system after signing minor league contracts and briefly appeared with the Cardinals’ top affiliate before closing out his playing career in the Dodgers organization.

While Bates only played 11 games in the Dodgers’ system in 2014, that proved to be a serendipitous landing spot. The Dodgers gave him his first coaching opportunity in 2015 after he retired as a player. Bates was a minor league hitting coach and coordinator before climbing to the big league staff as an assistant hitting coach in 2019. Bates and Robert Van Scoyoc have jointly carried the title of “hitting coach” with the Dodgers since 2023.

articles.title: Cardinals Promote Rob Cerfolio To General Manager
body: 9:40am: The Cardinals have formally announced Cerfolio’s promotion.

8:40am: The Cardinals are promoting assistant general manager Rob Cerfolio to the title of general manager, reports Derrick Goold of the St. Louis Post-Dispatch. He’ll serve as the No. 2 executive under president of baseball operations Chaim Bloom.

Cerfolio, 34, joined the Cardinals two offseasons ago. He’d previously been the Guardians’ director of player development and was given the title of AGM with a focus on player development and performance. He’s held that role for the past two seasons and now climbs another rung on the ladder.

It’s perhaps no coincidence that Cerfolio receives this title bump (and presumably pay increase) after his name emerged as a candidate in the Athletics’ GM search. He’s one of several known candidates that interviewed, joining Brewers assistant GM Matt Kleine and, of course, Red Sox assistant GM Taylor Smith, who ultimately landed the president of baseball operations title with the A’s. Cerfolio’s promotion to the GM post in St. Louis means that in order to be hired away by another organization in the future, he’d likely need to be offered a new team’s president of baseball ops title himself.

articles.title: Poll: Will Jake Bauers Accept The Qualifying Offer?
body: Earlier this week, eight players received a qualifying offer worth $23.15MM. Arguably, Jake Bauers was the most surprising name on the list. Whether he will accept that QO or not is one of the most interesting stories of the early offseason. Arguments can be made in either direction.

Two years ago, Bauers had one foot out the door of baseball. From 2018 to 2024, he bounced around the league, playing for the Rays, Guardians, Mariners, Yankees and Brewers. Teams clearly saw the talent but Bauers couldn’t put it all together. After the 2024 season, he had a career line of.208/.302/.361. That wasn’t in a small sample. He had stepped to the plate 1,744 times at that point.

Going into 2025, Bauers was projected by MLBTR contributor Matt Swartz for an arbitration salary of $2.3MM. The Brewers didn’t want to pay him that, so they put him on waivers. The other 29 clubs passed. Bauers became a free agent. He recently told Curt Hogg of the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel that he was planning to retire at that time while his wife would return to teaching, but then she became pregnant, so Bauers decided to keep playing. He returned to the Brewers on a minor league deal.

articles.title: Tarik Skubal Rumors: Mets, Dodgers, Cubs
body: Free agency opened to all 30 teams on Monday evening, officially kicking off the bidding for Tarik Skubal. The first few days of the offseason have been characteristically slow throughout the entire market, but there’s been early speculation about the landing spot for the top free agent.

Much of the attention has unsurprisingly focused on the Mets and Dodgers, generally viewed as the two likeliest Skubal destinations. Jon Heyman of The New York Post wrote on Wednesday that the Mets are indeed interested in making a run, though he cautioned they haven’t yet determined how far they’re willing to go in the bidding two years into the record-setting Juan Soto contract.

New York also has needs at the back of the bullpen and around their infield. The Dodgers are more well set up for luxury buys. They’ll need to re-sign or replace a few leverage relievers (Evan Phillips, Alex Vesia, Blake Treinen and Kris Bubic) and could poke around the second base market for an upgrade on Tommy Edman and Alex Freeland. They’re much better positioned than the Mets in prioritizing a handful of targets rather than addressing various roster needs.

articles.title: Rays, Levi Stoudt Agree To Minor League Deal
body: The Rays are in agreement with right-hander Levi Stoudt on a minor league contract with a non-roster invite to Spring Training, reports Marc Topkin of The Tampa Bay Times. Topkin also reported this week that Tampa Bay was re-signing righty Kodi Whitley with a camp invite.

Stoudt, who’ll be 29 next month, has four games of major league experience. Those came with the 2023 Reds, for whom he tossed 10 1/3 innings of 11-run ball. Stoudt subsequently spent time in the Baltimore organization and was on a minor league contract with the Phillies for 2026. He was out to a great start to the season, combining for 22 2/3 frames without an earned run between the top two minor league levels. There’s a decent chance he’d have earned himself a look in the Philadelphia bullpen had he not suffered an elbow injury in June that ended his season.

A third-round pick by the Mariners in 2019, Stoudt got some prospect attention early in his career on the strength of a mid-90s fastball and good control. He averaged 96 mph on his fastball in Triple-A this year but threw his mid-80s slider at a massive 85% clip. The pre-injury results were encouraging, as Stoudt struck out 11 of 39 Triple-A opponents while allowing a total of six baserunners in 11 innings.

articles.title: Braves To Hire Perry Minasian As Senior Advisor
body: The Braves are bringing Perry Minasian back to their front office, reports Bob Nightengale of USA Today. Jesús Cano of The Athletic reports that Minasian will be a senior advisor in amateur scouting.

That’s the same role that Dana Brown took when he rejoined the Braves’ front office last week. Minasian and Brown were both high-ranking Atlanta staffers — Brown as vice president of scouting, Minasian as assistant general manager — before getting opportunities to run AL West rivals. The Angels hired Minasian as their GM over the 2020-21 offseason; Brown got the same job with the Astros three years later.

Both executives were dismissed by their former clubs within a couple months of one another over the summer. The Angels fired Minasian in late June and hired John Mozeliak on an interim basis. Houston moved on from Brown in August, and while the team technically announced it as a mutual parting of ways, owner Jim Crane has made clear it was essentially a unilateral decision.

Brown and Minasian are experienced talent evaluators who clearly still have the trust of longtime Atlanta president of baseball operations Alex Anthopoulos. Minasian also had scouting experience with the Blue Jays when Anthopoulos was running the Toronto front office.

articles.title: Blue Jays To Have Fourth Option On Jake Bloss
body: The Blue Jays will have a fourth option for right-hander Jake Bloss, reports Shi Davidi of Sportsnet. That’s an important development for the club, as it will make it easier to keep Bloss on the roster next year.

Normally, a player has three option years. If a player on the 40-man roster is optionable, a team can send him to the minors without exposing him to waivers. If the player spends at least 20 days of a season on optional assignment, he uses up one of those options.

However, a team can be granted a fourth option on a player if he has exhausted the first three and hasn’t yet played five full seasons. A “full” season is one in which the player is active for at least 90 days, majors and minors combined, or one in which the player was active for 30 days and his active/injured list time added up to at least 90 days. Basically, these parameters are to exclude short-season rookie ball campaign as “full” seasons, or situations where a player misses an entire year due to a significant injury.

Those distinctions are moot with Bloss. He was only drafted by the Astros in 2023. He has only participated in four professional seasons, so it doesn’t really matter whether those were considered “full” or not. Houston gave him a roster spot in June of 2024, less than a year after he was drafted. He was traded to the Blue Jays a few weeks later as part of the Yusei Kikuchi deadline deal. The Blue Jays optioned him after that trade, so Bloss used his first option that season.

articles.title: Royals Hire Hunter Mense As Hitting Coach
body: 4:20pm: Feinsand further clarifies that Mense and Marcus Thames will be the hitting coaches in Kansas City while Connor Dawson will be offensive coordinator. In 2026, Thames and Dawson worked as hitting coaches alongside Alec Zumwalt. It was reported in September that Zumwalt would be reassigned to a position as senior director of hitting performance.

2:20pm: The Royals are hiring Hunter Mense as an assistant hitting coach, reports Mark Feinsand of MLB.com. Reporting from Mark Feinsand and Maria I. Guardado of MLB.com initially identified Mense as Kansas City’s new hitting coach.

Mense, 42, makes a quick pivot. It was less than a year ago that he got his first hitting coach job when the Giants hired him. He worked under first-time big league manager Tony Vitello, who had just been hired about a month earlier out of the college rangs. Now Mense is packing his bags for Kansas City.

Mense is a Missouri guy. He was born in Liberty and later played college ball at the University of Missouri. After his time playing at Missouri, Mense was drafted by the Marlins in 2006. He played minor league ball in Miami’s system for several years but never cracked the majors. He spent some time in independent ball before pivoting to coaching, working for the Blue Jays in the minor leagues. He got promoted to Toronto’s big league staff in 2022 as assistant hitting coach.

articles.title: Mets To Hire Johnny Washington As Co-Hitting Coach
body: The Mets are hiring Johnny Washington as a co-hitting coach, reports Joel Sherman of The New York Post. He was working for Atlanta in 2026 as minor league hitting coordinator.

Washington, 42, was drafted by the Rangers in 2003. He played in that club’s minor league system through 2006 but never played in the majors. He bounced around for a bit, playing some independent and minor league ball, with his last official game action coming in 2009.

He pivoted to coaching after that. He worked in the minors for the Dodgers and Padres. The latter club promoted him to first base coach on the big league staff for the 2017 season. He was named hitting coach for the 2019 campaign. He spent the 2021 season as the hitting coach for the Hanwha Eagles in the KBO. He returned to MLB in 2022, working as assistant hitting coach for the Cubs. He then served as hitting coach for the Angels in 2024 and 2025 before joining Atlanta this year.

The Mets fired manager Carlos Mendoza during the 2026 season. Andy Green replaced him on an interim basis. In September, the Mets and Green announced an extension that would keep him around for the next three seasons. Washington and Green overlapped in San Diego for a time, as Green was the manager of the Padres from 2016 to 2019.

articles.title: White Sox Sign Alec Marsh To Minor League Deal
body: The White Sox have signed right-hander Alec Marsh to a minor league contract with an invite to major league camp in spring training. Scott Merkin of MLB.com was among those to report the deal.

It’s an injury bounceback flier for the Sox. Marsh, 29 in May, was once a prospect of note with the Royals. Kansas City selected him with the 70th overall pick in 2019. Baseball America then ranked him as the club’s #23 prospect in 2020, before having him in the 10-15 range from 2021 to 2023.

Marsh went to toss 203 1/3 innings for the Royals over the 2023 and 2024 campaigns, making 33 starts and ten relief appearances. He allowed 4.96 earned runs per nine. His 23.4% strikeout rate and 8.8% walk rate were around league average but he struggled with the long ball. He allowed 35 home runs in that time, a rate of 14.6% per fly ball. League average is usually 11-12% but Kauffman Stadium tends to be on the pitcher-friendly side.

He hasn’t pitched in the big leagues since then. Heading into the 2025 season, Marsh experienced some soreness in his throwing shoulder. He began the campaign on the injured list with a shoulder impingement. He hit setbacks in his attempts to ramp up. He required labrum surgery in November of 2025 and spent the entire 2026 season on the IL.

articles.title: Red Sox Adding Shelley Duncan To Coaching Staff
body: The Red Sox are adding former big leaguer Shelley Duncan to their major league coaching staff, Chris Cotillo and Sean McAdam of MassLive.com report. As with Boston’s previously agreed-upon hiring of Jason Bell (who’d been with the Astros), a specific title has yet to be settled upon.

Duncan, 47, played in parts of seven big league seasons from 2007-13, totaling 330 games and 997 plate appearances as a first baseman and corner outfielder. He’s had a long coaching career in the more than decade that has passed since he called it quits as a player.

The Diamondbacks hired Duncan as a manager in the low levels of their system back in 2015. He spent a few seasons there before the Blue Jays hired him as their field coordinator ahead of the 2019 season. Duncan has also worked with the White Sox organization as their analytics coordinator and was most recently with the Yankees as the manager for their Triple-A affiliate in Scranton/Wilkes-Barre, where he was named the 2025 International League Manager of the Year.

Boston cleaned house on its coaching staff back in April, firing then-manager Alex Cora and five members of his staff on the heels of a terrible start to the season. Their own Triple-A skipper, Chad Tracy, was elevated to the big league manager’s role on an interim basis. After the Red Sox embarked on a remarkable turnaround under Tracy and made the postseason, Tracy was signed to a three-year contract as the Red Sox’ new skipper, shedding the “interim” label.

articles.title: Blue Jays, Rudy Martin Jr. Agree To Minor League Deal
body: The Blue Jays are bringing speedy outfielder Rudy Martin Jr. back on a minor league contract, Ari Alexander of 7News reports. He’ll be in big league camp as a non-roster invitee ahead of the 2027 season.

Toronto originally acquired Martin, 30, on waivers from the Orioles in August. He’d previously been with the Royals but gone to Baltimore in exchange for cash. The well-traveled minor league veteran made his big league debut with Toronto late in September but only tallied three plate appearances. He didn’t notch his first MLB hit but did draw a walk during those three trips. The Jays removed Martin from the 40-man roster last week, after which he elected free agency, but he’s now back with the organization as a depth option.

Martin spent the bulk of the 2026 season in Triple-A, tallying 369 minor league plate appearances between the Royals and Jays organizations. He posted a combined.274/.394/.421 (119 wRC+) between those two clubs. Martin homered 11 times and swiped 45 bags in 53 attempts (84.9% success rate). It’s been more than 12 years since the Royals drafted Martin in the 25th round out of Lewisburg High School in Missouri. He’s a career.252/.358/.387 hitter with 239 steals in nearly 2500 minor league plate appearances.
