articles.title: Angels Select Nicolò Pinazzi
body: The Angels announced that they have selected the contract of left-hander Nicolò Pinazzi. They also announced they have turned down a club option on righty Robert Stephenson, a move that was covered earlier today. Meanwhile, right-hander Jack Kochanowicz was reinstated from the 60-day injured list in a procedural move. He is recovering from Tommy John surgery and will be out until the second half of 2027, so he’ll go back on the 60-day IL once it becomes available again after the offseason.

Pinazzi, 27, hasn’t taken the typical path to a roster spot with the Angels. Born in Italy, he was signed by the Reds back in 2020. He was with that club through 2023 but was released before the beginning of the 2024 season. He spent a couple of seasons pitching in indy ball and then signed with the Halos for the 2026 campaign.

His numbers this year have been outstanding. Across four different levels, he tossed 64 innings over 48 appearances, allowing 0.84 earned runs per nine. His 12.5% walk rate is certainly high but he struck out 38.9% of batters faced and induced grounders on 60.8% of balls in play, those latter two both being excellent figures.

Brendan Gawlowski of FanGraphs profiled Pinazzi back in August. The lefty’s fastball sits in the mid-90s but he throws his breaking ball more than half the time. Pinazzi calls this pitch a cutter but admits the label is wrong. “I say cutter, but it’s definitely a slider,” he said. “I say cutter to delude myself, I throw more strikes that way.” Gawlowski notes that Pinazzi also mixes in a curveball but this cutter/slider is the money pitch.

articles.title: Guardians Select Milan Tolentino
body: The Guardians announced that they have selected the contract of infielder Milan Tolentino. They also declined a club option on right-hander Trevor Stephan as well as their end of a mutual option with righty Shawn Armstrong.

Tolentino, 25 next month, was a fourth-round pick in the 2020 draft. The fact that the Guardians are adding him to the roster now suggests he was about to qualify for minor league free agency. By giving him a roster spot, they prevent him from getting away.

He has never really been a top prospect in the system but he clearly has some tools. He has spent the past two years at the Triple-A level. He has stepped to the plate 957 times in that span, hitting 42 home runs and drawing walks at a strong 12.5% clip. The flipside is that he has also struck out as a massive 32.9% pace. That has led to a lopsided.221/.321/.445 batting line and 100 wRC+, indicating his offense works out to league average on the whole.

Defensively, Tolentino has spent most of his time at shortstop while also getting lots of action at second and third base. He very briefly dabbled in the outfield this year. The Guards have Travis Bazzana at second and José Ramírez at third. Shortstop could be covered by either Brayan Rocchio or Ángel Genao. Daniel Schneemann is on the roster and could be in a bench/utility role.

Tolentino will try to push into that mix but he has a full slate of options and could be in line for more time at Triple-A. He already has a couple of seasons at that level but it wouldn’t hurt to get some more seasoning in an attempt to cut down on the punchouts.

articles.title: Giants Outright Andrew Knizner
body: The Giants announced that catcher Andrew Knizner has cleared waivers and been sent outright to Triple-A Sacramento. He has the right to elect free agency and will presumably do so.

San Francisco entered the offseason needing to do a lot of roster maintenance. Eligible players become free agents as the offseason begins but the injured list goes away five days after the end of the World Series, meaning guys on the 60-day IL need to retake roster spots. As of a few days ago, RosterResource projected the Giants for a 40-man roster count of 56 once the IL was gone. Since then, they have been trimming things down. They lost Grant McCray and Braxton Roxby via waivers and outrighted Matt Gage, Jason Foley and Osleivis Basabe.

Knizner is the latest cut. The Giants signed him in August while Jesús Rodríguez and Daniel Susac were injured. Knizner shared the catching duties with Drew Cavanaugh down the stretch. Knizner got into 29 games and hit.219/.288/.356 with subpar defensive grades.

He finished the season with his service count between five and six years. He could have been retained for 2027 via arbitration, with MLBTR contributor Matt Swartz projecting him for a $1MM salary. The Giants have instead moved on, allowing them to clear a roster spot in what is effectively an early non-tender. They will hope that Susac, Rodríguez and Cavanaugh can handle things behind the plate next year, though they could also upgrade that group with an external addition.

articles.title: Diamondbacks To Hire Ben Fritz As Pitching Coach
body: The Diamondbacks have a new pitching coach. Dennis Lin of The Athletic reports that Arizona has snaked Ben Fritz away from the Padres. He has been working as the bullpen coach in San Diego. The Snakes parted ways with pitching coach Brian Kaplan earlier this month.

Fritz, 45, was a first-round pick of the Athletics back in 2002. He pitched in the minors through 2008 but never made it to the big leagues. He kept pitching in indy ball through 2010. The Padres gave him a minor league coaching job in 2015. He got the bullpen coach job at the big league level ahead of the 2020 season. He was briefly the pitching coach in 2021. Larry Rothschild was fired from that job in August of that year. Fritz held the job the rest of the way and then Ruben Niebla was hired in October.

For what it’s worth, the Padres have had good results in the pitching department in recent years. From 2020 to 2026, San Diego pitchers posted a collective 3.86 earned run average, behind just six other clubs. The Diamondbacks had a 4.55 ERA in that same time frame, better than just three teams.

It’s always tough to determine how much credit or blame to give to an individual coach, since he can only work with the players on the roster and is also just one member of a larger staff. But it seems Fritz has a good reputation in the league. He reportedly drew some interest from other clubs last year. Lin’s report from today notes that the Rockies were interested in him for their pitching coach vacancy but the Diamondbacks have managed to bring him aboard.

articles.title: Rays Decline Mutual Option On Cedric Mullins
body: The Rays announced that they have declined mutual options on right-hander Nick Martinez and outfielder Cedric Mullins. Both are now free agents. It was reported earlier that Martinez had turned down his end of his option.

It has been over a decade since a mutual option was triggered by both sides. They are mainly put into contracts as de facto deferrals. The buyout isn’t paid until the end of the season, allowing the team to delay some the guaranteed money in the deal. The Rays signed Mullins to a one-year deal last offseason. The $7.5MM guarantee was broken down as a $7MM salary and then a $500K buyout on a $10MM mutual option.

It was a buy-low move for the Rays. Mullins had some good seasons with the Orioles but was coming off a down year in 2025. He hit 17 home runs and had a 10% walk rate but slashed.216/.299/.391 for a wRC+ of 94. His.253 batting average on balls in play was below average, perhaps leaving room for positive regression.

His 2026 with the Rays was a mixed bag. His defensive numbers were strong but his offense got worse. His BABIP slid even farther to.227. His walk rate dropped to 8.6% and his homer total dropped to 15. He ended the year with a.205/.284/.344 line and 76 wRC+.

It wasn’t a great platform season but Mullins was good in the field. He was credited with six Defensive Runs Saved, 11 Outs Above Average and a grade of 10 from Fielding Run Value. The free agent market for center fielders is pretty weak, so Mullins will still be one of the better options available.

articles.title: Joc Pederson Declines Mutual Option With Rangers
body: Designated hitter Joc Pederson is back on the open market. Jesse Rogers of ESPN reports that Pederson has declined his end of an $18.5MM mutual option with the Rangers. He is now a free agent.

As with all mutual option decisions, this is essentially a procedural move. It’s been more than a decade since any of these were exercised by both parties. They’re generally a way for the team to delay paying a portion of the guaranteed contract in the form of a buyout, which isn’t due until the end of the season. They’re essentially an unofficial deferral within the contract term.

Pederson’s option was a little bit different, as there’s no buyout. It was effectively put into place as a method for the Rangers to override Pederson’s ability to opt out of his two-year contract last offseason. If he’d opted out, the Rangers could preemptively trigger the 2027 mutual option and retain him for 2026-27. It ended up being a moot point, as Pederson slogged through a miserable’25 campaign and never considered walking away from this year’s $18.5MM salary.

He finds himself in a quite different situation this time around. Pederson had a much better second season in Arlington, ranking second on the team with 26 home runs. He was their primary leadoff hitter against right-handed pitching and batted.245/.338/.496 across 396 plate appearances with the platoon advantage.

articles.title: Athletics Decline Club Options On Jeffrey Springs, Jeff McNeil
body: The Athletics announced that they have declined club options on left-hander Jeffrey Springs and infielder/outfielder Jeff McNeil. Both players are now free agents.

Neither decision is too shocking. Both players are 34 years old and coming off disappointing seasons. The A’s acquired Springs from the Rays in December of 2024. At the time, their rotation was mostly young and inexperienced. The A’s signed Luis Severino and acquired Springs in the hopes of providing some veteran stability.

Springs was fine enough in his first season with the A’s. He logged 171 innings and posted a 4.11 earned run average. Considering that the club was playing in a hitter-friendly minor league park, that wasn’t too bad. His 19.4% strikeout rate was subpar but his 7.6% walk rate was good. He got a bit of help from a low.255 batting average on balls in play.

Just about everything went in the wrong direction in 2026. His BABIP ticked up closer to average, landing at.278. His strikeout rate dropped to 17.8% and his walk rate climbed to 9%. The dimensions at Sutter Health Park became a problem. He allowed 35 home runs on the year, 23 of those at home. The 35 number was seven more than the previous season despite pitching almost 30 fewer innings. The end result was a 6.18 ERA.

articles.title: Mariners’ Michael Arroyo Undergoes Elbow Scope Procedure
body: The Mariners announced that Dr. Keith Meister performed an elbow scope on second baseman/left fielder Michael Arroyo two days ago. The procedure was meant “to clean up cartilage and brace a chronic injury to [Arroyo’s] UCL,” and the top prospect “is anticipated to be ready to return to game participation in April 2027.”

The projected timeline means Arroyo should begin next season on the injured list, though hopefully without too much time missed. It wasn’t guaranteed that Arroyo would’ve made the Opening Day roster even when healthy, as he has played only 49 games at the Triple-A level.

That said, Arroyo already hit.283/.359/.471 in 532 combined plate appearances at the Double-A and Triple-A levels in 2026. This production earned Arroyo his first promotion to the majors in September, and he hit the ground running with a very impressive.371/.439/.514 in his first 41 trips to the dish against MLB pitching.

While obviously a very small sample size, there’s plenty of optimism that Arroyo can be part of the Mariners’ next wave of young talent. Arroyo was an international signing in 2022, and his ability to generate plenty of hard contract has drawn him some top-100 prospect attention in the last two seasons. He has played only second base and left field over the last three years, so he could be a candidate to platoon with Cole Young at the keystone or get some time in left should Randy Arozarena depart in free agency.

articles.title: Mariners To Hire CJ Gillman As Hitting Coach
body: The Mariners are set to hire CJ Gillman as the new hitting coach, according to The Athletic’s Ken Rosenthal, Chandler Rome, and Spencer Nusbaum. Gillman formerly worked as Seattle’s minor league hitting coordinator from 2022-25, before spending last season as the Nationals’ director of hitting.

Kevin Seitzer worked as the Mariners’ hitting coach in 2025-26 before being let go at season’s end, as part of a wider staff shake-up that included three other coaches and manager Dan Wilson. Gillman is the first new name appointed to one of those staff vacancies, ahead of even a new skipper (though Joe Espada and Jason Kanzler are reportedly the two finalists for the job).

The next manager will surely get some input on the 2027 coaching staff, but as the Athletic trio note, it makes sense that the Mariners would want to lock Gillman in place now. Beyond his prior knowledge of the M’s organization, Gillman seemed to make a big impact in his one year in Washington, as part of the Nats’ system-wide overhaul once Paul Toboni took over as president of baseball operations. The director of hitting role generally takes a broader view of a team’s organizational hitting approach, and the Nationals greatly improved at both the major and minor league levels in 2026.

articles.title: Twins Decline Mutual Option On Josh Bell
body: Twins designated hitter Josh Bell is officially a free agent, the MLBPA announced today. His contract had a $10MM mutual option with a $1.25MM buyout. The team declined their end of the option, per Aaron Gleeman of AaronGleeman.com. Gleeman adds that the Twins declined their end of a 2027 mutual option for right-hander Joe Ryan, but Ryan remains under club control for next year via arbitration.

It’s not a surprise result in either case. It has been over a decade since a mutual option was picked up by both parties. They are mostly put into free agent contracts to delay part of the payment until the end of the season. The Twins signed Bell last winter to a one-year deal with a $7MM guarantee. That broke down as a $250K signing bonus, a $5.5MM salary and a $1.25MM buyout on the option. That structure allowed the Twins to delay part of the payment until now but it was always designed to be a one-year arrangement.

He will now head to free agency in search of his next home. He is still pretty solid with the bat. The switch-hitter made 631 plate appearances for the Twins this year. His 8.2% walk rate was just a hair below average, while his 19.7% strikeout rate was more that two ticks better than par. He hit 21 home runs and slashed.255/.319/.419 for a wRC+ of 106. That was his fourth straight season finishing with a wRC+ in the 102-106 range.

articles.title: Orioles Re-Sign Rece Hinds
body: The Orioles announced that outfielder Rece Hinds has been re-signed to a one-year Major League contract. The Baltimore Banner’s Andy Kostka reports that Hinds’ salary will be $4700 more than the next MLB minimum salary, which will be established when the next collective bargaining agreement is settled.

Hinds was first acquired by the O’s in a trade deadline deal with the Marlins in August, and was already under team control for 2027 and beyond. This new guaranteed deal locks in a place for Hinds on the 40-man roster for now, and Orioles president of baseball operations Mike Elias has often used this tactic in locking up players on the fringes of the roster.

With a guaranteed salary slightly beyond the league minimum, Hinds might be a little less appealing to teams looking to make a waiver claim if Baltimore designates him for assignment later this winter. This increases the chance that Hinds will clear waivers and then be outrighted off the 40-man roster. Hinds is out of minor league options, so the Orioles must first DFA the outfielder whenever they wish to remove him from the 40-man roster.

A second-round pick for the Reds in 2019, Hinds spent his whole career in Cincinnati’s organization until this past May, when he was designated for assignment by the Reds and then acquired by the Marlins for cash considerations. Hinds only appeared in one big league game during his two-plus months with Miami, in between 13 games with the Reds in 2026 and 12 games with Baltimore.

articles.title: Orioles Decline Mutual Option On Zach Eflin
body: Right-hander Zach Eflin was listed in a batch of new free agents in a press release from the MLB Players Association. That indicates that Eflin’s 2027 mutual option was turned down. Ronald Blum of The Associated Press reports that Baltimore passed on their end of the provision.

It’s not a surprising development. It has been over a decade since a mutual option was picked up by both sides. They are mostly used as accounting measures. Putting a buyout on a mutual option allows a club to defer some of the player’s payment to the end of the season, as opposed to be being paid out during the campaign as salary.

The O’s re-signed Eflin last winter to a one-year deal with a $10MM guarantee. That was broken down as a $3MM signing bonus, $5MM salary and $2MM buyout on a huge $25MM mutual option. The fact that the mutual option price was more than twice the guarantee illustrates that it was never really intended to be picked up. It just allowed the O’s to delay paying the final $2MM until this week.

Eflin had some incentives baked into the buyout price. If he had made 15 starts, he would have added $1MM, then $1.5MM more at 20 starts and an additional $2.5MM at 25 starts. Those escalators quickly became moot. Eflin was pulled in the fourth inning of his first start of the season with elbow discomfort. He underwent Tommy John surgery in early April. He spent the remainder of the season on the 60-day injured list.

articles.title: Angels Decline Club Option On Robert Stephenson
body: The MLBPA announced that Robert Stephenson is now a free agent, indicating that the Angels declined their $2.5MM club option on his services for 2027. Stephenson’s tenure in Los Angeles will now end with only 10 innings pitched over three seasons.

A trade from the Pirates to the Rays in June 2023 suddenly turned Stephenson in a dominant bullpen weapon, as he posted a 2.35 ERA, 5.7% walk rate, and a stunning 42.9% strikeout rate over 38 1/3 innings in a Tampa Bay uniform. Though his overall numbers over eight MLB seasons had been much less consistent, the Angels believed that Stephenson’s breakout was legit, and he was signed to a three-year, $33MM free agent deal in January 2024.

Unfortunately for Stephenson and the Halos, he barely got a chance to prove himself on the mound. He missed all of 2024 and some of 2025 recovering from Tommy John surgery, and also battled biceps and elbow inflammation that limited him to just the 10 frames in 2025. More elbow problems emerged last spring, and Stephenson underwent a ligament and flexor repair procedure in April that kept him on the shelf for all of 2026.

The TJ procedure unlocked a clause in Stephenson’s contract that gave the Angels this extra club option year for 2027. Though $2.5MM isn’t a large sum, the team might have further concerns about Stephenson’s health, or the Angels just want to move on entirely from this failed signing. Former GM Perry Minasian signed Stephenson under the approval of owner Arte Moreno, though Minasian was fired last season and Moreno has now sold the team to Stan Kroenke’s ownership group.

articles.title: Matthew Boyd, Carson Kelly Decline Mutual Options
body: Cubs lefty Matthew Boyd and catcher Carson Kelly are now free agents, the MLBPA announced Friday. Both players had mutual options — Boyd’s valued at $15MM and Kelly’s at $7.5MM. Boyd receives a $2MM buyout, while Kelly will receive a $1.5MM buyout. Ronald Blum of The Associated Press reports that both players declined their end of the mutual provisions. They’re now free agents who’ll be free to explore opportunities with other teams beginning early next week. In the meantime, they can talk with the Cubs about potentially re-signing in Chicago.

Boyd, 36 in February, missed a chunk of the 2026 season when he required arthroscopic surgery to fix a partial meniscus tear. He posted good results when healthy, logging 126 2/3 innings with a 3.91 ERA, 18.5% strikeout rate, 7.5% walk rate and 42.2% ground-ball rate.

Boyd managed only 202 2/3 innings from 2021-24 due to a series of injuries — most notably Tommy John surgery. He was healthy at the tail end of the’24 campaign, however, which prompted the Cubs to place a medium-scale (two years, $29MM) bet that he could bounce back to his typical midrotation form. That bet paid off, as Boyd wound up making 53 starts and pitching 306 1/3 frames with a 3.50 ERA, 20.2% strikeout rate and 6.5% walk rate.

articles.title: Red Sox Decline Mutual Option On Sonny Gray
body: Sonny Gray is officially a free agent, as the MLBPA included the right-hander’s name on a list of players who have resolved their club or mutual options heading into the offseason. Ronald Blum of The Associated Press reported that the Red Sox declined their end of the option. Gray would surely have opted out anyway, so that’s essentially a procedural move.

Gray will pocket a $10MM buyout and now head to the open market on the heels of a very successful season in Boston. With the Cardinals heading into a full-on rebuild last winter, Gray agreed to waive his no-trade clause and approved a deal that sent him to the Sox last November. Gray then delivered a 2.72 ERA and 6.7% walk rate over 29 starts and 169 innings for the Red Sox, helping stabilize the rotation even after Garrett Crochet missed most of the season.

Though he is turning 37 in a week’s time and is entering his 15th MLB season, Gray made it clear that he plans to return for at least one more go-around in 2027. It seems likely that Gray will be able to command two guaranteed years in his next contract, though he could prefer the flexibility of a one-year contract given that he has lightly hinted at retirement on the horizon. Reports have indicated that Gray would prefer to pitch for teams on the East Coast or in relative proximity to his home in Nashville, so those clubs might have a bit of an advantage in pursuing Gray this offseason.

articles.title: Blue Jays Outright Rudy Martin Jr.
body: The Blue Jays announced that Rudy Martin Jr. has been outrighted to Triple-A Buffalo after clearing waivers. Since Martin has been outrighted in the past, he has the ability to reject the assignment and opt for free agency.

It hadn’t been made public that Martin had been designated for assignment, but the outfielder has now been removed from the Jays’ 40-man roster. This drops Toronto’s roster down to 38 players, which gives the Blue Jays some extra space to make some acquisitions in advance of Monday’s deadline for 40-man roster compliance. Some other teams have way more than 40 players, leaving the Jays in position to swing some trades or make some waiver claims.

Martin is a veteran of 11 pro seasons, spent mostly in the Royals’ farm system but also with stints in the Nationals’ minor league ranks, and stops in independent ball and the Mexican League. He was also briefly a member of the Orioles’ organization after being acquired from Kansas City in July, but Martin never actually played for the O’s, as he was quickly DFA’ed and then claimed by the Jays within a week of leaving the Royals.

The 30-year-old was then again designated and outrighted off Toronto’s 40-man after clearing waivers, but Martin’s time finally came in September. The Blue Jays selected his contract to the active roster and Martin appeared in two games in a Toronto uniform, finally making him a Major League player. After debuting as a late-game pinch-runner, Martin started in left field the next day and drew a walk in his three plate appearances.

articles.title: Diamondbacks Seeking Controllable Starting Pitching
body: After deciding whether or not to trade Ketel Marte, a secondary item on the Diamondbacks’ to-do list will be adding to the rotation. General manager Mike Hazen tells Nick Piecoro of The Arizona Republic that he would like to acquire a controllable starter. That is more likely to happen via trade, as Hazen is unlikely to push hard for a starter in free agency given the team is planning to reduce payroll.

The D-backs had a middling 4.28 ERA out of their rotation this year. The group’s 9.6% K-BB rate bested only the lowly Rockies, as Arizona’s starters showed good control but struggled to strike opponents out. Eduardo Rodriguez was better than expected. He posted a 2.89 ERA over 32 starts despite middling peripherals and led the staff with 3.2 fWAR. Michael Soroka and Brandon Pfaadt were the next best performers after him. Both had ERAs below 3.40, with Soroka riding an above-average 24.1% strikeout rate and Pfaadt relying on ground balls and control.

The trouble is that Soroka will become a free agent once he declines his end of a $10MM mutual option. Both sides have expressed interest in a reunion, though it remains unclear how far Arizona will go to retain Soroka while also addressing the rest of their roster. The bullpen, first base, and left-handed hitting all need to be addressed, as MLBTR’s Anthony Franco wrote in our Offseason Outlook series.

articles.title: Marlins Exercise Club Option On Sandy Alcantara
body: One of the most straightforward option decisions for any team this offseason is now official. The Marlins announced Friday that they’ve exercised their $21MM club option on right-hander Sandy Alcantara. It’s a net $19MM decision, as the Marlins would have owed Alcantara a $2MM buyout even if they’d preferred to move on and let the face of their franchise test free agency. The 2027 campaign will be the last year he’s under contract. He’s slated to become a free agent next winter.

There was never a doubt that this option would be picked up. Alcantara had a strong rebound in his second season back from Tommy John surgery. Major League Baseball’s consummate workhorse tossed 214 innings — tops in either league — and notched a 3.87 earned run average. Alcantara’s 17.1% strikeout rate was well below average, but his 6.6% walk rate was strong and his 41.9% ground-ball rate was about average.

Because of the Marlins’ perennially small payroll and frequent rebuilds, Alcantara’s name has come up in trade chatter at seemingly every turn over the years. That’s far less likely to be the case this winter, even as he heads into his final year of contractual control.

The Marlins reportedly have no interest in trading Alcantara and have every intent of keeping him and starting him on Opening Day once again next season. President of baseball operations Peter Bendix has spoken of Alcantara’s importance to the club on multiple occasions, and he’s unsurprisingly said to be a personal favorite of owner Bruce Sherman.

articles.title: Marlins Outright Five Players
body: The Marlins’ offseason housekeeping has begun. Miami has outrighted five players off the 40-man roster, according to the team’s transaction log at MLB.com. Catchers Logan Driscoll and Brian Navarreto and righties Tyler Zuber, Wikelman González and Zach Brzykcy have all cleared waivers. They’re all likely headed to minor league free agency.

The two catchers saw little to no big league time this year. Driscoll, 29 next week, didn’t appear in the majors. The Marlins added him in a cash swap with Tampa Bay just prior to the deadline. He was a depth option with the Rays and remained in that role with Miami. Driscoll raked in 14 Triple-A games for the Fish but was below-average the rest of the season with the Rays’ top affiliate. Overall, he hit.269/.367/.422 in 77 games at the Triple-A level. His only big league work to date was a 15-game cup of coffee with the 2024 Rays, wherein he batted.171/.189/.257 with a homer in 37 plate appearances.

Navarreto, 32 in December, totaled 61 plate appearances with Miami this year. He hit just.135/.193/.250 with a homer. Navarreto was originally a sixth-round pick by the Twins in 2013. He’s split his entire career between the Minnesota and Miami organizations, appearing in parts of three seasons with the latter. He’s a well below-average hitter even in Triple-A, but Navarreto is a strong defender and seasoned minor league vet who could be re-signed to give the Fish some glove-first depth to keep at their top minor league affiliate.

articles.title: Nick Martinez Declines Mutual Option With Rays
body: Nick Martinez declined his end of a $20MM mutual option with the Rays, reports Jon Heyman of The New York Post. Martinez will collect a $4MM buyout and return to free agency.

The outcome was always certain. Mutual options are used as accounting measures and are almost never picked up by both sides. Even if Martinez opted in, it’s possible the low-spending Rays would have declined their side of the option, or otherwise picked it up before trying to trade Martinez. MLBTR’s Payroll Tracker projects the club for a $105.6MM cash payroll in 2027. Martinez would have bumped up that total by $16MM (the difference between the option price and the buyout).

The 36-year-old Martinez may not get a $20MM average annual value on the market, but he should find a decently paying two-year deal with a higher total guarantee. Tampa Bay brought him in on a $13MM salary back in February. Martinez then delivered his best season as a full-time starter in the big leagues.

Over 31 starts and 180 innings, Martinez held opponents to a 3.10 earned run average. Despite a below-average 15.1% strikeout rate, he thrived as the league’s premier control specialist. Martinez only gave up free passes 3.6% of the time, beating out teammate Drew Rasmussen and Braves lefty Chris Sale (both at 4.8%) for the best mark among qualified starters. ERA estimators like FIP (3.96) and SIERA (4.63) weren’t as bullish on Martinez, while FanGraphs gave him 2.9 wins above replacement, valuing his mid-rotation performance.

articles.title: Diamondbacks Expected To Field Interest On Ketel Marte
body: The Diamondbacks’ biggest offseason question is whether they’ll line up a Ketel Marte trade. Arizona fielded interest in the star second baseman early last offseason, though it seemed mostly a matter of due diligence as they explored ways to add controllable starting pitching.

There’s a good chance the team will more aggressively shop Marte this offseason — albeit with various reasons why it may be more difficult to actually make a deal. Most notably, Marte can veto any trade after securing 10-and-5 rights (10 years of service time, the last five with one club) in April.

Reports from both John Gambadoro/Alex Weiner of Arizona Sports and Nick Piecoro of The Arizona Republic indicate that the Snakes will explore Marte trades yet again. Piecoro writes that they’ve received preliminary interest from other clubs, though it’s obviously very early in the process with the trade market just reopening this morning.

Marte features prominently on MLBTR’s list of the game’s top offseason trade candidates, slotting in at #6. That’s driven in large part by comments from team officials who’ve become increasingly frustrated with Marte no-showing for certain games over the years.

articles.title: Red Sox Re-Sign Angel Bastardo To Minor League Deal
body: The Red Sox are re-signing reliever Angel Bastardo to a minor league contract with an invite to big league camp, reports Francys Romero. The 24-year-old righty would otherwise have qualified for minor league free agency next week.

Bastardo has been in affiliated ball since 2018. The Venezuela native began his career on a modest $35K signing bonus. Bastardo eventually developed into a borderline top 30 prospect in the Boston farm system, though his ascent up the minors was halted by Tommy John surgery in 2024. That led the Red Sox to leave him off the 40-man roster when he was eligible for the Rule 5 draft. The Blue Jays selected him and stashed him on the injured list for the entire’25 season.

Toronto kept Bastardo on their 40-man into Spring Training. He and Spencer Miles were both vying for spots in the bullpen as Rule 5 selections. Toronto wasn’t going to carry two Rule 5 picks in a year where they hoped to contend, though, and Miles outperformed Bastardo in Spring Training. The Jays sent Bastardo back to the Red Sox, who assigned him to Triple-A Worcester.

Bastardo made 40 appearances for the WooSox. He worked 54 1/3 innings of 4.64 ERA ball, striking out a strong 32% of opponents but issuing walks at an untenable 14.3% rate. He averaged 96.2 mph on his fastball and leaned on a changeup as his best secondary pitch, sporadically mixing in a slider and curveball. Bastardo will try to earn a spot in Chad Tracy’s relief group next spring.

articles.title: Red Sox To Trade Tsung-Che Cheng To Tigers
body: The Red Sox are trading infielder Tsung-Che Cheng to the Tigers for cash, reports Andrew Parker of Sox Prospects. He’ll occupy a spot on Detroit’s 40-man roster, which is up to either 42 or 44 depending on their option decisions for Drew Anderson and Kenley Jansen.

Boston, which already cleared one spot by trading Nate Eaton to the Athletics this afternoon, will be at 42 once Sonny Gray declines his end of a mutual option and becomes a free agent. Both teams will need to drop down to 40 by Monday evening.

Cheng spent one season on the Sox’ roster. Boston claimed him off waivers from the Nationals in February. The Taiwanese infielder made a three-game debut with the Pirates last year and bounced around the waiver wire over the 2025-26 offseason. He played a minimal role in Boston, starting 13 games at shortstop amidst a monthlong stint on the MLB roster. He hit.256 with one extra-base hit, a double, in 44 plate appearances.

The 25-year-old Cheng spent the remainder of the season on optional assignment to Triple-A Worcester. He posted a league average.241/.345/.390 slash with eight home runs. Cheng rarely expanded the strike zone and walked at a strong 14% clip. He struck out at a slightly elevated 24% rate and didn’t hit the ball with much authority. Prospect evaluators have generally praised his plate discipline and solid defensive chops around the infield, projecting him as a utility piece. He’s out of minor league options and will battle for a bench job in Detroit if he holds his 40-man spot all offseason.

articles.title: Phillies To Designate Garrett Stubbs For Assignment
body: The Phillies informed catcher Garrett Stubbs that he’s being designated for assignment, reports Scott Lauber of The Philadelphia Inquirer. They’ll have five days to trade him or place him on waivers once they officially announce the DFA.

The move ends Stubbs’ five-year tenure with the organization. Philadelphia acquired the lefty-hitting backstop from the Astros in a minor trade over the 2021-22 offseason. Stubbs operated as the backup catcher behind J.T. Realmuto for the next three seasons. He’s fallen to third on the catching depth chart in the last two years, as Rafael Marchán has held the reserve role.

Philadelphia ran the out-of-options Stubbs through waivers at the end of Spring Training. That came after they unsuccessfully tried to find a taker on the trade front. He came back up in mid-April when Realmuto landed on the injured list. Philadelphia operated with three catchers once Realmuto returned, using Stubbs as the last player off the bench. He missed a week and a half in July to left wrist inflammation but otherwise held a spot on the active roster for the final five months of the season.

Stubbs only made it into 35 games. He started 17 times behind the plate and once in left field, otherwise coming off the bench. The USC product batted.153 without a home run in 65 plate appearances. He finishes his Philly tenure with a.212/.292/.300 slash in 181 contests. The likely outcome is that Stubbs will clear outright waivers and opt for minor league free agency.

articles.title: Dustin May Declines Mutual Option With Brewers
body: Dustin May declined his end of a $20MM mutual option with the Brewers, reports Jon Heyman of The New York Post. He’ll collect a $500K buyout and return to the open market.

This was a formality, as mutual options are essentially never triggered by both sides. (Milwaukee would likely have passed on their end of the $20MM provision as well.) May signed a one-year, $12.5MM free agent deal with the Cardinals last winter. St. Louis flipped him to the Brewers alongside reliever JoJo Romero, netting a pair of high-upside outfield prospects for the impending free agents.

The Brewers obviously have no complaints as they celebrate their first championship. Romero proved the more valuable of the two acquisitions from St. Louis, though. May allowed a 5.65 ERA across 36 2/3 regular season innings for the Brew Crew. He gave up seven runs over 11 frames during the playoffs.

It was an up-and-down season for the 29-year-old righty. May finished the year with a combined 4.70 ERA but established a career high with 145 2/3 innings. He struck out a solid 23.2% of opponents against a league average 8.1% walk rate. May has a six-pitch mix and averaged nearly 97 mph on his fastball. Teams have continually been intrigued by the arsenal, so he should do reasonably well in free agency.

articles.title: Brewers Notes: Contreras, Megill, Vaughn
body: For the first time in their 57-year history, the Brewers are World Series champions. Perennially a contender despite bottom-tier payrolls and contributions from unheralded players, Milwaukee broke through with an disciplined offense (MLB-best 10.6% walk rate), terrific defense and baserunning, and a powerhouse bullpen that supported a rotation fronted by the NL’s likely Cy Young Award winner.

It’s party time in Milwaukee for the time being, but the celebration can’t last long. The offseason begins today, and with it, critical decisions that will shape their chances of defending the World Series crown.

The Brewers’ model by now is well known. They ponied up to sign Christian Yelich long-term back in March 2020, and they’ve more recently extended top prospects like Jackson Chourio, Aaron Ashby, Cooper Pratt and Luis Lara before they ever even played in the majors. Chourio, Pratt and Lara hadn’t even taken a single big league plate appearance when the trio signed respective long-term contracts guaranteeing them $82MM, $50.75MM and $31MM.

articles.title: Mets Claim Kyren Paris From Angels
body: The Mets announced they’ve claimed infielder/outfielder Kyren Paris off waivers from the Angels. New York also designated outfielder Cristian Pache for assignment.

Paris, who turns 25 next month, is a former second-round pick who has played parts of four big league seasons. He’s a good athlete with speed and raw power who’ll need to dramatically cut down on the strikeouts to even carve out a career as a bench player. The righty-swinging Paris owns a.147/.238/.272 slash line with seven home runs and 11 stolen bases across 263 career plate appearances. He has gone down on strikes in 38% of his trips to the plate.

New York is evidently intrigued enough by the tools and Paris’ minor league production. While he barely factored into the Halos’ big league plans this season, he’s coming off a.274/.384/.458 showing with 13 homers and 24 steals between Double-A and Triple-A. Paris has played mostly middle infield in his minor league career but has the speed to factor into the outfield mix as well.

This was Paris’ final minor league option season. He’ll either need to break camp or be placed back on waivers at some point before Opening Day. The latter outcome is more likely, and there’s a decent chance the Mets will attempt to sneak him through waivers during the offseason.

articles.title: Braves Exercise Options On Ronald Acuña Jr., Ozzie Albies
body: The Braves announced they’ve picked up their options on Ronald Acuña Jr. and Ozzie Albies. Acuña will make $17MM next season, while Albies will match this year’s $7MM salary. Those were Atlanta’s only option decisions this year.

There wasn’t much suspense with either decision. The Braves weren’t going to cut either member of their core for what would’ve amounted to $7MM in savings. Acuña’s option came with a $10MM buyout that meant he’d only have been bought out had he suffered some kind of career-altering injury. Albies’ deal didn’t have a buyout but comes with a base salary akin to what solid utility infielders (e.g. Isiah Kiner-Falefa, Willi Castro) make as free agents.

The Braves have Acuña until team control for two seasons, as there’s another $17MM option on his deal for the 2028 campaign. That one doesn’t have a buyout, so it’d be a costlier decision, but it’s still highly likely to be exercised. Acuña hit 20 homers with a.255/.345/.451 slash line in a relative down year. He’s one season removed from a monster.290/.417/.518 showing after coming back from the second ACL tear of his career.

This will be the final season of the $35MM extension that Albies signed early in his career. Atlanta has tacked on $10MM by picking up two club options along the way — a $4MM buyout on his first option was already factored into that $35MM guarantee — so he made a total of $45MM over a nine-year stretch. Albies handily outperformed those salaries, though he’s been more serviceable than great going back to the start of the 2024 season.

articles.title: Caleb Durbin Undergoes Foot Surgery
body: The Red Sox announced that Caleb Durbin underwent surgery on the fifth metatarsal in his right foot (relayed by Christopher Smith of MassLive). It’s the second postseason operation for the third baseman, who also had a minor procedure on his left pinky finger a few weeks ago.

Boston didn’t reveal a recovery timetable, but there’s no indication either surgery is expected to impact his readiness for Spring Training. They mostly serve to confirm that Durbin was playing through a few different injuries down the stretch. Despite the health concerns, the 26-year-old infielder was much better in the second half than he’d been early in the season. Durbin’s first two months in Boston were ugly enough that it came as a moderate surprise that the Sox didn’t option him to Triple-A.

The front office was rewarded for its faith. Durbin caught fire in June and July. While his power numbers dropped again in the final two months of the season, he continued to reach base at a strong clip. Durbin finished the year with a league average.248/.332/.378 batting line with 13 home runs in aggregate. The Sox will hope for something closer to the.279/.369/.424 slash he posted after June 1 as he enters his second season at Fenway Park.

articles.title: Athletics Outright Six Players
body: The Athletics announced that six players have been sent outright to Triple-A Las Vegas, indicating that they recently cleared waivers. They are right-handers Henry Baez, Joey Estes and Geoff Hartlieb, catcher Brian Serven, infielder Michael Stefanic and outfielder Johnathan Rodríguez.

As the offseason begins, many teams are facing roster crunches. Free agency begins today for eligible players, which opens some breathing room. But the injured list goes away five days after the World Series ends. Coming into today, RosterResource projected the A’s for a count of 46 for the offseason. Then they acquired Nate Eaton in a trade with the Red Sox. These six moves get the club down to 41.

Estes, 25, is one of the more experienced players in the group. He gave the A’s 127 2/3 innings back in 2024 with a 5.01 earned run average. Since then, he has mostly been kept in the minors as a depth arm, only making five big league appearances over the past two seasons. His Triple-A ERA was north of 5.50 in both of those campaigns. He exhausted his final option season and will be out of options going forward. He has at least seven years in the minors, meaning he’ll qualify for minor league free agency in the coming days.

articles.title: Royals Exercise Club Option On Tony Gonsolin, Decline Carlos Estévez
body: The Royals announced that they have exercised a 2027 club option on right-hander Tony Gonsolin. He will make $2.5MM next year. Right-hander Carlos Estévez has had his $13MM club option turned down. He becomes a free agent and collects a $2MM buyout.

Gonsolin is a relatively low-cost wild card for next year’s staff. From 2019 to 2023, he tossed 375 2/3 innings for the Dodgers, allowing 3.19 earned runs per nine. He had a 23.1% strikeout rate, 8.7% walk rate and 38.8% ground ball rate.

He hasn’t been much of a factor since then. He required Tommy John surgery in August of 2023, wiping out the end of that season and his 2024 campaign. In 2025, he suffered a back injury while lifting weights. He began the season on the injured list. He came off the IL in April, made seven starts with an ERA of 5.00, then returned to the IL with elbow discomfort. He would eventually require internal brace surgery in August.

He was bumped from the Dodgers roster after the season. He was still recovering from his surgery when the 2026 campaign began. He didn’t sign until August. The Royals gave him a prorated $1MM salary and a $2.5MM club option for 2027. He made four minor league rehab appearances before joining the big league club. He made one appearance in the majors, allowing five earned runs in 2 2/3 innings, before an allergic reaction put him back on the IL in late September.

articles.title: Giants Outright Three Players
body: The Giants outrighted left-hander Matt Gage, right-hander Jason Foley and infielder Osleivis Basabe off the 40-man roster, per a team announcement. San Francisco also lost outfielder Grant McCray and righty Braxton Roxby on waivers — McCray to the Mariners and Roxby to the Nationals.

Gage and Foley are veteran relievers who’ve run into injury troubles. Elbow problems limited the former to only 27 1/3 innings this year, during which he posted a 5.60 ERA with an unsightly 17.5% strikeout rate and 13.5% walk rate. He’d been effective in parts of three prior seasons, logging a 2.66 ERA in 50 2/3 innings between the Jays, Astros, Tigers and Giants — albeit with a roughly average 22% strikeout rate and a higher-than-average 9.8% walk rate.

Gage had a 1.96 ERA through the season’s first two months before being mauled for 12 runs in his final 4 1/3 innings. He’s reportedly expected to have a normal offseason, but the Giants had a staggering 16 players on the 60-day injured list and need to open a huge number of roster spots, so Gage will fall to the wayside.

articles.title: Twins Outright Three Players
body: The Twins removed three players from their 40-man roster Thursday, passing lefty Anthony Banda, first baseman Aaron Sabato and infielder Tristan Gray through waivers. The team announced the moves.

None of the three are terribly surprising. Banda had a decent season out of Minnesota’s bullpen after coming over in a trade with the Dodgers, who’d designated him for assignment. However, he suffered a torn lat midseason that required surgery and is expected to sideline him well into next year. MLBTR contributor Matt Swartz had projected the lefty for a $2.3MM salary in his final year of club control. It’s possible the Twins will look to bring him back on a minor league deal, but they understandably weren’t willing to carry him on the 40-man roster all winter and pay him a guaranteed salary north of $2MM when he’s facing a lengthy injury absence and would’ve been slated for free agency following the 2027 season.

When healthy, Banda logged 34 1/3 innings with a 4.46 ERA, 21.2% strikeout rate, 9.6% walk rate and 39.2% ground-ball rate. He had a slow start in his new setting but had been on a roll when the injury bug bit; in his final 20 1/3 frames of the season, Banda notched a sparkling 1.33 ERA with 20 punchouts and 10 walks. He also gave the 2024-25 Dodgers 114 1/3 innings of 3.14 ERA ball. Banda has more than five years of big league service, so he’ll elect free agency.

articles.title: Mariners Claim Grant McCray
body: The Mariners have claimed outfielder Grant McCray off waivers from the Giants, according to announcements from both clubs. The Mariners say their 40-man count is now at 35 though players on the 60-day injured list will need to be reinstated by Monday. RosterResource projects Seattle for a 40-man count of 43 for the offseason, including McCray.

A lot of teams are doing roster maintenance at this time of year. Free agency began today, opening some 40-man spots. But as mentioned, the IL goes away five days after the end of the World Series. The Giants are in a fairly extreme spot in this regard. As of this morning, RosterResource pegged them for a 40-man count of 56. Putting McCray on waivers was just one of many moves they will have to make this week. As mentioned, the Mariners also have to do some roster maneuvering, but they will grab McCray with the openings they currently have.

McCray, 26 in December, was a third-round pick of the Giants back in 2019. He was added to the 40-man roster late in 2024. Since then, he has served as up-and-down outfield depth, getting shuttled between the majors and Triple-A. In 102 big league games, he has stepped to the plate 247 times and produced an ugly.170/.235/.323 line. But Statcast put his sprint speed in the 95th percentile of qualified players this year. In his career, McCray has stolen 13 bags without getting caught.

articles.title: Nationals Claim Braxton Roxby, Designate Zak Kent
body: The Nationals have claimed right-hander Braxton Roxby off waivers from the Giants and designated fellow righty Zak Kent for assignment, the club announced Thursday.

Roxby, 28 next spring, made his major league debut with the Giants in 2026. He tossed 5 1/3 innings and allowed a pair of runs on six hits and two walks with three strikeouts. The former Reds farmhand landed in San Francisco as part of the 2025 Taylor Rogers trade. He spent the majority of the 2026 season in Triple-A Sacramento, where he posted a 3.78 ERA, 23.1% strikeout rate, 10% walk rate and 38.9% ground-ball rate.

Roxby works off a three-pitch mix featuring a four-seamer, sinker and slider. The slider was his primary pitch both in the minors in both 2025 and 2026, and that held true in his big league cup of coffee. Since he was just selected to the majors for the first time late in the 2026 season, Roxby still has a full slate of three minor league option years remaining. He’s not a lock to last the entire offseason on the Nationals’ 40-man roster, but he’ll compete for a spot in a wide-open bullpen mix if he makes it to camp with Washington in 2027.

Kent, who’ll turn 29 in February, split the 2026 season between the Nationals and Twins organizations after bouncing around the waiver circuit for much of the 2025-26 offseason. He pitched 16 1/3 big league innings but was roughed up for a 5.51 ERA. He pitched well in a small sample with the Twins’ Triple-A club but posted pedestrian numbers with Washington’s top affiliate in Rochester.

articles.title: Corbin Burnes Will Not Opt Out Of Diamondbacks Deal
body: Right-hander Corbin Burnes will not take the opt-out chance in his contract with the Diamondbacks, reports Bob Nightengale of USA Today. He will make $35MM annually through the 2030 season, though $11MM is deferred annually.

There wasn’t any suspense with this decision. Burnes and the Snakes agreed to a six-year, $210MM deal in December of 2024. His agent Scott Boras would later suggest that he turned down larger offers from other clubs because his family has a home in Scottsdale.

The first two years of the agreement have mostly been wasted. Burnes made 11 starts in 2025 before requiring Tommy John surgery. He was hoping to make it back around the 2026 All-Star break but suffered a teres major strain in June, delaying his timeline. He came off the injured list in September but made just three starts, with a 7.84 earned run average, before shoulder inflammation put him back on the shelf.

Burnes is very talented and has a Cy Young trophy on his mantel but it would have been unwise to turn down $140MM with that kind of platform. The family/geography considerations made it even less likely.

He will return to the Arizona rotation in 2027 and hope for better results going forward. It’s possible he may face workload restrictions after missing most of the past two years. Time will tell on that. On paper, he’s in the rotation next to Eduardo Rodríguez, Brandon Pfaadt, Merrill Kelly and Ryne Nelson. The Snakes and Michael Soroka have mutual interest in a reunion. Even if Soroka doesn’t come back, they will likely bring in someone else to bolster the group.

articles.title: Astros Decline Club Option On Ryan Weiss
body: The Astros have declined a $5MM club option on right-hander Ryan Weiss, reports Jesse Rogers of ESPN. Weiss will collect a $500K buyout as he returns to free agency.

Weiss spent 2024 and 2025 putting up good numbers in South Korea. Over those two seasons, he tossed 270 1/3 innings for the Hanwha Eagles with a 3.16 earned run average. In the latter season, he made 30 starts with a 2.87 ERA, 28.6% strikeout rate, 7.7% walk rate and 48.5% ground ball rate.

The Astros tried to bring him to North America as a cheap rotation addition. They signed him to a one-year deal with a $2.6MM guarantee in the form of a $2MM salary in 2026, a $100K signing bonus, and a $500K buyout on a $5MM club option for 2027.

It didn’t work out. Weiss made nine appearances, posting a 7.62 ERA through 26 innings. His 22.9% strikeout rate was around average but he walked 15.3% of batters faced. He was designated for assignment in June and cleared waivers. He also tossed 76 1/3 Triple-A innings with a lackluster 5.42 ERA. Given that season, it’s unsurprising that the Astros aren’t bringing him back next year. He’ll now look for his next opportunity. If he stays in North America, he should be limited to minor league offers. If he gets another chance to pitch overseas, he might be tempted to take it.

articles.title: Mariners Announce Three Option Decisions
body: The Mariners announced Thursday that they’ve exercised their $9MM club option on closer Andrés Muñoz. Seattle declined a $6.075MM club option on righty Bryce Miller and a $9MM club option on outfielder Victor Robles.

Miller remains under club control through 2029 via arbitration. The one-year deal he signed when avoiding arbitration last offseason included a club option for his second arbitration season. However, with a $3.9MM projected arbitration salary for Miller (via MLBTR contributor Matt Swartz), the M’s will pay a small $15K buyout on 2026’s option and instead broker a new deal in arbitration. Robles, meanwhile, receives a $500K buyout and is now a free agent.

The 27-year-old Muñoz is coming off a career-worst season that saw him pitch to an uncharacteristically high 4.24 ERA while blowing 10 of the 39 save/hold situations handed to him by the team. Despite the rocky showing, the M’s will give him another look, which isn’t particularly surprising when considering the price of free agent relievers and, more importantly, the fact that his contract contains a similarly affordable $10MM option for the 2028 season.

Despite the glut of blown opportunities, Muñoz averaged 99.8 mph on his heater — his best mark since 2022’s career-high 100.2 mph — and punched out a massive 37.1% of his opponents. His 10% walk rate was worse than average, but not necessarily by an egregious amount. That also represents his best mark since a dominant 2022 campaign.

articles.title: Tatsuya Imai Will Not Opt Out Of Astros Deal
body: Right-hander Tatsuya Imai will not opt out of his deal with the Astros, reports Jon Heyman of The New York Post. He will make $18MM in both 2027 and 2028, though he will have another opt-out chance a year from now.
Imai was first making the move from Japan to North America last winter. His final seasons in Nippon Professional Baseball were dominant, as he posted an earned run average around 2.00 in those.

However, he had struggled with control for most of his career, posting walk rates well north of 10% in many seasons. He got that down to 9.8% in 2024 and then 7% in 2025, leading to some optimism that he had turned a corner in that department. But on the other hand, the NPB had a dead ball in those years, which may have made it easier for Imai to just fill up the zone and not get burned.

There was some thought that Imai’s upside might allow him to secure a nine-figure deal. It seems the uncertainty with his profile prevented him from getting there. He secured a three-year, $54MM guarantee from the Astros. That deal featured opt-outs after each season, giving Imai the path to greater earnings down the line if he hit or approached his ceiling.

One year in, it seems the concerns were warranted. Imai struggled badly with control and eventually got pushed to the bullpen. He finished the season with 76 2/3 innings pitched over 15 starts and eight relief appearances. He had a huge 28.7% strikeout rate but gave out walks at a massive 15.1% pace. The end result was a 4.93 earned run average.

articles.title: Athletics Acquire Nate Eaton From Red Sox
body: The offseason trading has begun. The Athletics have acquired outfielder Nate Eaton from the Red Sox in exchange for minor league right-hander Jareth Rayo. Bob Nightengale of USA Today first reported that Eaton was traded to the A’s. Chris Cotillo of MassLive first reported the Sox would get a minor leaguer in return. Francys Romero of BeisbolFR first identified Rayo.

Eaton, 30 in December, was on the roster bubble in Boston. He served an up-and-down depth role this year, getting shuttled between Triple-A and the majors. He hit just.160/.300/.260 in the big leagues and exhausted his final option season. It was going to be hard for him to a hold a spot on the 40-man through the offseason.

Most teams are facing a crunch in the coming days. The injured list goes away on Monday, meaning several players on the 60-day IL will need to retake roster spots. Prior to this deal, RosterResource projected the Sox for a 40-man count of 44, factoring in players coming off the IL and those bound for free agency. They still have to open three spots but moving Eaton starts the process of alleviating the logjam.

It is perhaps not a coincidence that the A’s have a new front office leader who just departed Boston. General manager David Forst was dismissed in August. In October, the club hired Taylor Smith as president of baseball operations. Smith had previously been an assistant general manager with the Red Sox and should be familiar with Eaton.

articles.title: Diamondbacks Considering First Base Work For Nolan Arenado
body: The Diamondbacks and third baseman Nolan Arenado are thinking about him playing first base next year, reports Steve Gilbert of MLB.com. This wouldn’t be about moving Arenado off the hot corner, but the extra versatility could help the club’s offseason pursuits while also keeping him healthier.

Arenado just wrapped up his age-35 season and he will turn 36 in April. His third base defense is no longer at the elite levels of earlier in his career but remains passable, depending on your metric of choice. Defensive Runs Saved was the most bearish on his 2026 work, giving him a grade of minus-four. On the other end of the spectrum, Outs Above Average and Fielding Run Value had him in positive territory, with both of those metrics giving Arenado a grade of two above par.

Though he has never played any other position, it’s understandable that the Diamondbacks would want to contemplate making him viable at first. First base is generally considered a less taxing position than third base, something the Snakes are thinking about as Arenado is squarely in his mid-30s. “I think it’s taken a toll on him physically a little bit,” general manager Mike Hazen said. “So we’re trying to be mindful of that.”

articles.title: Offseason Outlook: Milwaukee Brewers
body: In their 57th season in existence, the Brewers captured their first World Series championship. The team hopes it’ll take only one more season to land title #2, as Milwaukee is in good position to make another run.

articles.title: Brewers’ Matt Kleine Is Astros’ Top Target In GM Search
body: The Astros are looking for a new general manager and may have found one. Chandler Rome of The Athletic reports that Brewers assistant general manager Matt Kleine is Houston’s top choice, though a deal to officially hire him has not yet been agreed upon.

Kleine has been in the mix for quite a while. Back in August, shortly after Dana Brown was dismissed from the Houston general manager position, Kleine was mentioned as a possible candidate. That report also mentioned Matt Klentak, another Milwaukee assistant general manager. Rome’s report today mentions that Klentak did indeed receive interest but removed himself from consideration earlier this month.

In the weeks and months that followed Brown’s dismissal, Kleine emerged as a real consideration, as expected. He wasn’t alone. Former Nationals president of baseball operations Mike Rizzo, Rays assistant general manager Kevin Ibach, White Sox assistant general manager Josh Barfield, Cardinals assistant general manager Randy Flores, Royals senior vice president Scott Sharp and Braves assistant general manager Ben Sestanovich were also publicly connected to the vacancy, though Kleine was viewed by many as a favorite.

It’s an understandable choice. As mentioned by Rome, Astros owner Jim Crane suggested he would be looking to find a new general manager within the ranks of a club that had been finding major league success with a low payroll.

articles.title: Ryan Helsley To Exercise Player Option
body: Orioles right-hander Ryan Helsley will exercise his $14MM player option and forgo a return to the open market, reports Andy Kostka of the Baltimore Banner. He’ll remain with the team through 2027 before becoming a free agent again next winter.

There was never any real doubt this would be the case. Helsley signed a two-year, $28MM deal with Baltimore last offseason on the heels of a poor finish to his 2025 season with the Mets. The second season of the contract was a player option. Injuries limited him to just 15 1/3 innings, and the longtime Cardinals closer finished out the 2026 season on the 60-day injured list due to discomfort in his right elbow.

From 2022-24, Helsley was one of the most dominant relievers in baseball. He saved 82 games and tallied nine holds with St. Louis across those three seasons, pitching to a collective 1.83 ERA with a 34.6% strikeout rate and 9.2% walk rate. The flamethrowing righty averaged better than 99 mph with his heater during that time and regularly popped triple-digit readings on radar guns. His 17.4% swinging-strike rate across those three years was eighth-best among 185 qualified relievers.

articles.title: José Barrero Elects Free Agency
body: Orioles infielder/outfielder José Barrero was removed from the team’s 40-man roster and has elected free agency, reports Francys Romero of BeisbolFR.com. Presumably, that subtraction came by way of outright waivers. Barrero has been outrighted in the past and thus had the right to elect free agency upon clearing waivers.

The 28-year-old Barrero only appeared in two games with Baltimore this season. He went 1-for-6 with a single but spent the remainder of the year in Triple-A, where he batted.202/.305/.400 with 23 homers and 13 steals in 499 trips to the plate.

Barrero once ranked among the sport’s best prospects, climbing as high as No. 33 on Baseball America’s top-100 list ahead of the 2022 season. He was a high-profile signing out of his native Cuba, inking a $5MM signing bonus with the Reds back in 2017. He made his big league debut with Cincinnati in 2020 and has now appeared in parts of six big league seasons without any real production to show for it.

articles.title: Michael King Declines Player Option
body: Right-hander Michael King has declined his 2027 player option, reports Jon Heyman of The New York Post. He is now a free agent. Like the other 2026-27 free agents, King has a five-day window where he can only sign with his previous club, which is the Padres in King’s case. Those players will be free to sign with any club at 4:00 pm Central time on November 2.

King was a free agent last winter. He had posted strong results from 2023 through 2025 but went into the open market with questions about his health. Shoulder and knee injuries hampered him in the latter portions of the 2025 campaign. Due to the uncertainty with his health, he re-signed with the Padres on a relatively short pact but one that gave him the flexibility to re-enter free agency.

It was technically a three-year, $75MM guarantee. That broke down as a $12MM signing bonus, a $5MM salary in 2026, a $28MM player option for 2027 with a $5MM buyout, followed by a $30MM player option for 2028.

King went on to stay healthy in 2026. He threw 185 innings over 32 starts. His 3.21 earned run average was a slight improvement over his 3.44 mark in 2025. His strikeout and walk rates moved in the wrong direction but he got more ground balls. He then posted a 0.64 ERA over three postseason appearances.

articles.title: Brewers Win World Series
body: The Milwaukee Brewers are champions. They knocked off the Rays by a 4-1 margin tonight, securing the franchise’s first title. Milwaukee took down the Rays in five games to complete an 11-2 showing in October. They dispatched the Padres, Dodgers and Tampa Bay after winning an MLB-high 103 games in the regular season. William Contreras was named World Series MVP.

It’s a fitting end to the first 100-win season in club history. Milwaukee was baseball’s best team from the end of April. They opened the year by sweeping the White Sox, never dipped below.500, and took the lead in the NL Central by the middle of May. They’d never relinquish that advantage and cruised fairly comfortably to the top record in the league, three games clear of the Dodgers.

The Brewers played a tightly contested Division Series against San Diego, winning it in four despite every game being decided by one or two runs. That proved to be the closest they’d come to facing adversity this postseason, as they swept the Dodgers in the NLCS. They nearly did the same to Tampa Bay, though the Rays pulled off a 12th-inning comeback on Tuesday to prevent the Brew Crew from ending the playoffs on a nine-game win streak.

While Milwaukee won every series relatively comfortably, they did frequently need to pull themselves off the mat within games. The Brewers only opened the scoring in five of their 11 postseason victories. They’d generally erase the deficit by the middle innings, then lock down the lead with a deep and overpowering bullpen.

articles.title: The Braves’ Other Middle Infield Question
body: The Braves have the most glaring shortstop need in MLB. Mauricio Dubón and Ha-Seong Kim are impending free agents, leaving Jim Jarvis as the top in-house option. There’s a decent chance they’ll re-sign Dubón on a two-year deal, but he’s ideally suited as a super-utility player.

If the Astros make Jeremy Peña available before his year of club control, the Braves should be heavily involved. They’ll also surely look into younger shortstops who might be expendable on their current team (e.g. Anthony Volpe, Brayan Rocchio). The focus on shortstop has potentially overshadowed that the Braves’ other middle infield position might also need a shakeup.

Ozzie Albies has started 1117 games at the keystone for the Braves over the past nine seasons. No one else has started more than 44. Albies has been a steady, durable lineup fixture for years. He has handily outperformed the $35MM contract extension he signed in April 2019 and was a legitimate star through the’23 campaign.

articles.title: Astros Interview Oz Ocampo For Assistant General Manager Role
body: The Astros are reshaping their front office and the new look might include an old friend. Francys Romero of BeisbolFR reports today that Oz Ocampo interviewed for a job with the club. Specifically, Ocampo interviewed for an assistant general manager role and that interview took place on Monday, per Brian McTaggart of MLB.com.

Ocampo has a long history with the Astros, as he worked for the club from 2012 to 2020 and then again in 2022, primarily in the fields of international scouting and player development. As mentioned by McTaggart, he has been credited with being instrumental in many of Houston’s finds on the international market. McTaggart mentions Framber Valdez, Cristian Javier, José Urquidy, Luis Garcia, Bryan Abreu, Yuli Gurriel and Wilyer Abreu as some of his finds.

That track record was enough to get Ocampo opportunities elsewhere. He got a special assistant gig with the Pirates in 2019. He came back to the Astros after that but then got an assistant general manager job with the Marlins in October of 2022. He was let go from that post in August of 2024. He got a job with the Rockies in June, per Romero.

The Houston front office is currently in flux. General manager Dana Brown was dismissed in August. It was announced at that time that Brown’s duties would be split between assistant general managers Charles Cook, Gavin Dickey and Connor Huff, as well as senior advisor Jeff Bagwell, with owner Jim Crane overseeing the baseball operations department. Since then, the club has been looking for a new front office leader.

articles.title: Pirates Notes: Keller, Valdez, Buchanan
body: Mitch Keller’s season ended the day before the trade deadline, when the Pirates placed him on the 60-day injured list due to a teres major strain in his right shoulder. The team didn’t provide major specifics at the time, but Aiden Stepansky of MLB.com writes that Keller is believed to have suffered a Grade 3 strain — a gruesome injury that saw his teres major muscle detach from the bone.

Keller somewhat remarkably didn’t require surgery. Doctors recommended a lengthy down period and rehab. The plan has been for him to resume throwing late this month, and he’s expected to have a normal offseason.

The injury didn’t occur on one specific pitch, it seems. Keller told Stepansky he couldn’t pinpoint the exact moment at which it occurred. That suggests he was pitching through discomfort for some time, and the results bear that out. The typically steady Keller was dinged for a 5.29 ERA in 22 starts. His 17.7% strikeout rate was a career-worst, and his 8.3% walk rate — while still solid — was his highest since 2022. He posted a sub-7% mark each year from 2023-25. Keller’s 93.3 mph average fastball was also a career-low mark. He sat at a season-low 91.9 mph in his final start before hitting the injured list.

articles.title: Red Sox Adding Jason Bell To Coaching Staff
body: The Red Sox are hiring Astros major league field coordinator and outfield coach Jason Bell and adding him to their major league coaching staff, reports Brian McTaggart of MLB.com. Bell will serve as the outfield instructor, per Tim Healey of the Boston Globe, and the two parties are still sorting out the potential for additional responsibilities.

It’s the latest shuffling involving what should be a revamped Astros staff in 2027. Owner Jim Crane opted not to retain manager Joe Espada earlier this month and also dismissed five coaches while reassigning bench coach Omar Lopez to a new role within the organization. At the time, the Astros indicated that Bell was one of four coaches who’d be retained, joining pitching coach Josh Miller, hitting coach Victor Rodriguez and first base coach Dave Clark. Instead, it seems Bell was granted to interview for an opportunity in Boston and will now pack his bags for Fenway Park.

Bell, 36, joined the Astros organization as a development coach in 2017. He’s since managed in their minor league system, spent a half decade as the minor league field coordinator, and has now spent the past three seasons as a uniformed coach on the big league staff. The Astros were his first stop in pro ball, but he’s previously been the director of baseball operations for Ohio University and served as the pitching coach at the University of Maryland-Eastern Shore. McTaggart profiled Bell’s atypical path to a major league coaching staff back in 2024, when he was first hired.

articles.title: Tigers Re-Sign Carlos Perez To Minor League Deal
body: Veteran catcher Carlos Perez is headed back to the Tigers on a minor league deal, as relayed in a transactions update from Matt Eddy at Baseball America. Perez split the 2026 campaign between the Tigers’ and Astros’ Triple-A affiliates.

Perez, who turned 36 yesterday, has been in four different organizations over the past three seasons. He hasn’t received a big-league call at any of those stops. Houston signed him last offseason as a depth option behind Yainer Diaz and Christian Vazquez. Diaz missed time with an oblique strain over the summer, but it was César Salazar who got the call to replace him.

Houston released Perez in mid-June. After a brief stint in the Mexican League, he signed with the Tigers. Perez got off to a blazing start with Triple-A Toledo, hitting.351 with seven homers in his first 12 games. An ankle injury in early August cut his season short. It was only a 69-game sample, but Perez did finish with a 108 wRC+ and 15 homers in the minors this year.

Perez will reprise his role with the Mud Hens in 2027. He hasn’t reached the majors since 2023 with the Athletics. His 68 games with the club that season marked his first big-league opportunity since 2018. Perez has a.592 OPS across 859 MLB plate appearances. He was a plus behind the plate early in his career, but had a poor defensive season with the A’s.

articles.title: Latest On Cardinals’ Outfield Plans
body: The Cardinals are entering their second full season under president of baseball operations Chaim Bloom. St. Louis kicked off a retool once Bloom took over last winter and remained committed to that plan at the deadline despite hovering around the Wild Card picture.

St. Louis seems likely to take a similar approach next year as they remain focused on a long-term goal of building the starting pitching pipeline. The JJ Wetherholt extension is their only contract on the books, however, giving them plenty of short-term payroll capacity if they want to look outside the organization. They’ll surely bring in some help on the pitching staff and are open to a move at third base, where a group led by Nolan Gorman and Blaze Jordan was unproductive.

The rest of the Cardinals’ infield played well. They’re well positioned at catcher, designated hitter, and in right field. St. Louis ranked in the bottom third of the league in production from their left and center fielders. Those join third base as the biggest question marks in the Cardinals’ lineup, though it seems they’re less inclined to prioritize external outfield help.

articles.title: Dodgers Notes: Sasaki, Davalan
body: Dodgers right-hander Roki Sasaki made some progress in 2026 but wants to keep pushing next year. Per Dylan Hernandez of The New York Post, he wants to continue working as a starter and find enough success to be part of a playoff rotation. “In the playoffs, I think the team winning is prioritized more than anything,” Sasaki said. “I think that if I pitch well in the regular season, I should be able to throw (in the postseason). If I can’t do that, I think it would just mean I’m not good enough.”

Sasaki is two years into his big league career now. In both seasons, he was in the rotation mix during the regular season but got pushed into a bullpen role in the postseason. In both campaigns, his earned run average was a bit underwhelming, going from 4.46 last year to 4.49 in 2026. But the details around the ERA were more encouraging in 2026.

For one thing, the workload was far greater. A shoulder impingement put him on the injured list for most of 2025, limiting him to just 36 1/3 innings in the majors. In that time, his 17.4% strikeout rate, 13.7% walk rate and 38.9% ground ball rate were all worse than league average. In 2026, he did miss some time with a blister but cranked his innings tally up to 122 1/3. His 23.6% strikeout rate, 9.2% walk rate and 42.2% ground ball rate were all around average.

He also seemed to get better as the season went along. In the second half, he posted a 2.83 ERA in 41 1/3 innings, with a 25.3% strikeout rate and 8.8% walk rate. The challenge will be in putting up numbers like that consistently and over a full season.

articles.title: Offseason Outlook: Athletics
body: The A’s went from 76 wins in 2025 to a 64-98 record this year, as a swath of injuries and continued poor pitching threw a wrench into the rebuilding efforts. New president of baseball operations Taylor Smith is now tasked with getting the A’s back on track in their final year in Sacramento.
