articles.title: Orioles Notes: Front Office, Rotation
body: The Orioles’ offseason business is already well underway. The team announced last week that now-former Cubs assistant general manager Jared Banner has been named GM. He’ll work as the No. 2 executive under president of baseball operations Mike Elias, although Elias detailed to the team’s beat that they’ll have a pretty clear division of labor (link via Jake Rill of MLB.com).

While the two will collaborate overall, Banner will head up all things pertaining to the team’s in-house players, including “internal players, internal coaches, player development, performance, healthcare,” according to Elias. He added: “I think he’s better than I am in those areas.”

For his part, Elias will focus on scouting, player acquisition, contract negotiations and other big-picture aspects of the Orioles’ day-to-day operations. Elias didn’t tip his hand on what sort of personnel additions are still on the horizon, but the O’s will be open to further hires and Banner will spearhead those efforts. Banner noted that Orioles legend Cal Ripken Jr., who holds a minority stake in the ownership group and has been working with the team’s player development outfit, will continue to be “very involved” in the organization’s player development efforts (via Matt Weyrich of the Baltimore Sun).

articles.title: Joe Espada, Jason Kanzler Reportedly Finalists For Mariners Managerial Job
body: The Mariners’ managerial search may be coming to an end. Adam Jude and Ryan Divish of The Seattle Times report that former Astros skipper Joe Espada and Cubs director of player development Jason Kanzler are the finalists. Those two will have in-person interviews Tuesday and Wednesday. The report mentioned the possibility of the Mariners reaching out to coaches from the Rays or Brewers after the World Series is done but the Mariners are planning to name a new manager by the end of the week.

Both Espada and Kanzler have been connected to the job opening in previous reports but there were plenty of others in the mix and it now appears it is down to these two. The Times says there were 30 to 40 names on the initial search list and the club had conversations with many candidates. Rocco Baldelli was identified as one of them but he withdrew his name recently. Daniel Kramer of MLB.com reports that was likely due to geography, as Baldelli and his family live in Florida.

Kramer also reports that White Sox bench coach Walker McKinven and Rays senior advisor Brandon Hyde were also in the mix but no longer in the running. His report, which was published yesterday, noted that Espada and Kanzler would be getting in-person meetings but wasn’t clear if those two were considered finalists. Today’s reporting from The Times has many of the same details but goes a bit farther in framing Espada and Kanzler as finalists.

articles.title: Jeff Hoffman Undergoes Elbow Surgery; Expected To Be Ready For Next Season
body: The Twins announced that right-hander Jeff Hoffman has undergone arthroscopic surgery on his right elbow, a procedure that involved debridement and the removal of a bone chip. The club expects the righty to begin a throwing program in eight weeks and be ready for the start of the 2027 season. Dan Hayes of The Athletic passed the information along.

Hoffman, 34 in January, was acquired from the Blue Jays at this year’s trade deadline. The Twins were in the playoff race at the time and decided to make a postseason push, grabbing Hoffman from the Jays as well as Dean Kremer from the Orioles and A.J. Minter from the Mets. Unfortunately, Minnesota went 21-30 in August and September and finished seven games back of a playoff spot.

That slide was no fault of Hoffman’s, as he pitched well after the trade. He tossed 18 innings, allowing five earned runs for an ERA of 2.50. His 15.6% walk rate in that time was quite high but he punched out 35.1% of batters faced. Combined with his time with the Blue Jays, he finished the season with a 3.55 ERA, 34.9% strikeout rate, 10.3% walk rate and 44.7% ground ball rate over 66 innings.

Hoffman’s three-year deal, initially signed with the Blue Jays, still has one more season remaining. He’ll make $11MM next year but the Jays are paying $3.75MM of that as part of the trade, leaving the Twins on the hook for $7.25MM.

articles.title: Offseason Outlook: Washington Nationals
body: The Nationals overhauled many aspects of the organization in 2026. Changes in the front office and coaching staff produced the best season since the 2019 campaign, which ended in a World Series victory. Washington remained in the playoff race through July. The club sold at the trade deadline but should have plenty of opportunities to add this offseason.

articles.title: Phillies Hire Peter Fatse As Hitting Coach
body: Oct. 27: The Phillies have officially announced the Fatse hiring. The club is also adding Joe Cronin as an assistant hitting coach. Edwar Gonzalez will be back as an assistant hitting coach for a second season.

Oct. 26: The Phillies are going to hire Peter Fatse as their new hitting coach, reports Charlotte Varnes of The Athletic. He will replace Kevin Long, who was let go from the hitting coach position a couple of weeks ago.

Fatse, 39, was drafted by the Brewers in 2009 and played some minor league ball in that club’s system. He wound up in independent ball in 2011 and 2012 but that was the end of his playing career, at least as far as official game action goes.

He then pivoted to coaching. He got a minor league job with the Twins in 2019. After just one season, he was hired away by the Red Sox and given a big league job as assistant hitting coach. After the 2021 season, Boston and hitting coach Tim Hyers parted ways. Fatse was given the promotion to replace Hyers.

It’s always tough to parse out the contributions of a coach from the performance of the players. For what it’s worth, the Red Sox as a team hit.255/.322/.419 for a wRC+ of 104 from 2022 to 2025. The team got out to a slow start in 2026 which led to a mass firing. Manager Alex Cora and several coaches, including Fatse, were let go in April of this year.

articles.title: Nationals To Hire David Besky As Pitching Strategist
body: The Nationals are expected to hire David Besky as pitching strategist, per Kyle Williams of the Baltimore Banner. Besky most recently served as the director of baseball sciences for the Red Sox. Chris Cotillo of MassLive.com had previously reported that Besky was no longer with the team and was headed for a new gig.

It’s unclear whether Besky will be replacing anyone on the Nationals coaching staff. Given the report last week that manager Blake Butera’s crew was expected to return in 2027, it seems like this is a new addition, not a replacement. Washington didn’t have anyone with the pitching strategist title last season, but Sean Doolittle held the position in 2024 and 2025. He was promoted to assistant pitching coach this past year.

Spencer Nusbaum of The Athletic added this morning that Besky will be involved with pitch calling and arsenal analysis, among other duties. He’s been with the Red Sox for the past three seasons. Besky was originally hired as a player development coordinator. He took over as director of baseball sciences heading into the 2025 season. He overlapped with Nats president of baseball operations Paul Toboni, who was an assistant GM in Boston during Besky’s tenure. Before landing a job with the Red Sox, Besky spent three years as a data scientist at Driveline Baseball.

articles.title: Offseason Outlook: Philadelphia Phillies
body: The Phillies took a step back in 2026. After winning the NL East in 2024 and ‘25, they needed all 162 games this year to secure the NL’s final postseason berth. As a result, their talented starting rotation was stretched thin for the Wild Card round, and the Braves sent them packing. It’s now been three years since Philadelphia won a playoff series. This team is as deep in “win-now” mode as anyone, but the Phillies have plenty of questions to answer as they look to lengthen a top-heavy roster.

articles.title: A’s Max Muncy Undergoes Knee Debridement
body: The Athletics announced that infielder Max Muncy underwent a debridement surgery to address cartilage damage in his left knee. He also received a platelet-rich plasma injection. Muncy is expected to be fully ready for the start of camp.

Muncy finished the season on the injured list, missing the final week with the cartilage issue. It evidently required a minor procedure but shouldn’t have much impact on his offseason. Muncy is entering what could be a make or break season. He’s down to one minor league option year remaining and will need to impress a front office led by newly-hired president of baseball operations Taylor Smith, who doesn’t have the same attachment to Muncy as did former GM David Forst.

A first-round pick in 2021, Muncy has yet to establish himself in parts of two big league campaigns. He hit.214/.259/.379 as a rookie last year. Muncy’s numbers improved marginally in his sophomore season, as he batted.230/.296/.387 with nine homers across 284 plate appearances. He struck out at a concerning 32% clip while walking less than 8% of the time. Muncy has above-average bat speed but has yet to dial in a consistent enough approach against big league pitching. Twelve of his 18 career home runs have come against fastballs, and he’s struggled to make contact against any kind of secondary stuff.

articles.title: Mets To Add Mariano Duncan To Coaching Staff
body: The Mets are going to add Mariano Duncan to their major league coaching staff, reports Joel Sherman of The New York Post. Sherman doesn’t specify what title Duncan will have but says his duties will involve working with the position players in various facets. Separately, Mike Puma of The New York Post reports that Kevin Long is no longer under consideration for a role with the Mets. Chelsea Janes of SNY adds that Cubs assistant hitting coach John Mallee is also no longer in the mix.

Duncan, 63, spent over a decade in the big leagues as a player. From 1985 to 1997, he suited up for the Dodgers, Reds, Phillies, Yankees and Blue Jays. He was primarily a middle infielder but played every position on the diamond outside of the battery.

After his playing days ended, he pivoted to coaching. He has been in dugouts for more than 20 years now. He started in the early 2000s with some minor league work. He got his first major league coaching gig with the Dodgers in 2006 and held the first base coach job for that club through the 2010 season.

He then wound up back in the minors, serving as a hitting coach for farm clubs with various different franchises. He has been with the Mets recently. In 2019, he was hitting coach for the Rookie ball Kingsport Mets. After the minor leagues were cancelled in 2020, he served as bench coach for High-A Brooklyn in 2021. From 2022 to 2026, he was bench coach for Double-A Binghamton.

articles.title: Astros To Interview Mike Rizzo For GM Vacancy
body: The Astros are looking for a new general manager are going to interview longtime Nationals GM Mike Rizzo on Monday, reports Bob Nightengale of USA Today. Nightengale’s report also notes that Brewers assistant GM Matt Kleine, a known candidate, has already interviewed for the position.

Rizzo is easily the most experienced of the candidates who have been publicly connected to the Houston job, which has been vacant since Dana Brown was let go earlier this year. Rizzo was a longtime scout who got the top job in Washington in 2009. The Nats were rebuilding at that time and built up a strong core of young talent led by Bryce Harper, Stephen Strasburg and many others. Washington emerged as a contender in 2012 and stayed that way for the rest of the decade, winning the World Series in 2019.

In hindsight, it’s now clear that the championship season in 2019 was the end of the club’s competitive window. They fell below.500 in 2020 and have been under that line since. Juan Soto, Trea Turner, Max Scherzer and many other players were traded away in an attempt to pivot to a new core. The initial results on that reset were poor, so Rizzo was fired last year. The Nats then hired Paul Toboni, who had been assistant GM with the Red Sox and was 35 years old at the time, to run the front office in Washington.

articles.title: Did Anyone Win The Caleb Durbin Trade?
body: The deal that sent infielder Caleb Durbin from the Brewers to the Red Sox seemed like a disaster for two months. By the end of the year, it looked like a season-saving maneuver.

Boston and Milwaukee executed the six-player swap in early February. Durbin joined the Red Sox after the club came up short in an attempt to replace third baseman Alex Bregman in free agency. Fellow infielders Andruw Monasterio and Anthony Seigler, plus a draft pick, also came over in the deal. The Brewers received infielder David Hamilton and lefties Kyle Harrison and Shane Drohan.

Bregman’s departure in free agency left a big hole at third base. Durbin did not fill it, at least initially. He finished May with a.530 OPS. He had the second-lowest wRC+ among qualified hitters at that point in the season. Durbin was one of the key figures in Boston’s tumultuous first half. The club fired manager Alex Cora near the end of April after a 10-17 start. Interim manager Chad Tracy didn’t immediately right the ship.

While Durbin and the Red Sox scuffled, Harrison was thriving in Milwaukee. He was one of the most dominant pitchers in the early going, carrying a 1.57 ERA into June. Harrison raised his arm angle with the Brewers. He added induced vertical break to his four-seamer and got more drop on his slurve. The adjustments with his new team helped Harrison form an imposing one-two punch at the top of the rotation with ace Jacob Misiorowski.

articles.title: Royals Release Jorge Alfaro
body: Veteran catcher Jorge Alfaro was released by the Royals, per his MILB.com transaction tracker. Alfaro spent the 2026 season in the minors with Kansas City. He’ll head to free agency in search of another opportunity.

The 33-year-old Alfaro joined the organization on a minor league deal in December. He received an invitation to MLB Spring Training, but did not appear in a game. Alfaro was with Team Colombia in the World Baseball Classic, which was going on during spring action.

The Royals entered the year with a solid catching tandem in Salvador Perez and Carter Jensen. They cycled through veterans Elias Diaz and Luke Maile during the season with Perez banged up. Alfaro never got a look in the majors.

Alfaro slashed.223/.287/.468 in 62 games between Kansas City’s Double-A and Triple-A affiliates. He popped 15 homers and also stole a base. While the power production is impressive, Alfaro also struck out at a massive 41.5% clip.

Strikeouts have held Alfaro back for much of his career. He’s appeared in parts of nine MLB seasons with six different teams. Alfaro has punched out more than 30% of the time whenever he’s received semi-regular playing time. He has a 34% strikeout rate across 1,749 big-league plate appearances.

articles.title: Rocco Baldelli Withdraws Name From Mariners’ Managerial Search
body: Rocco Baldelli was a candidate to be the Mariners’ next manager, but the former Twins skipper has removed himself from the search due to “family considerations,” The Athletic’s Ken Rosenthal reports. The news leaves former Astros manager Joe Espada and Cubs director of player development Jason Kanzler as the only two known candidates remaining for the job, though other unknown names are reportedly in the mix.

The Mariners are apparently “in an advanced stage” in the hiring process, as Rosenthal, Chandler Rome, and Patrick Mooney put it earlier this week. If Baldelli was Seattle’s preferred choice, this could delay things if the team has to pivot to a second choice. Ex-manager Dan Wilson announced prior to the Mariners’ final game that wouldn’t be returning in 2027, so the team’s search for a new skipper has been officially ongoing for almost a full month. (Since the Mariners’ disappointing season made it increasingly likely that Wilson was on the way out, upper management was probably starting to start forming plans well in advance of Wilson’s announcement.)

President of baseball operations Jerry Dipoto hinted that hiring an experienced manager would be his preference this time around, rather than a first-time MLB skipper like previous hires Wilson or Scott Servais. Beyond Baldelli and Espada, Diamondbacks manager Torey Lovullo was reportedly on the Mariners’ radar before Arizona signed Lovullo to a new contract, and Guardians manager Stephen Vogt (who is under contract in Cleveland) made a point of publicly stating that he is staying put.

articles.title: Trade Candidate: Teoscar Hernandez
body: Teoscar Hernandez’s shaky 2023 season with the Mariners didn’t establish much of a platform as the outfielder entered free agency for the first time, and the result was a one-year, $23.5MM deal with the Dodgers. Hernandez chose the shorter-term contract over some lengthier offers with the intent of hitting well in 2024 and putting himself in better position to command a more lucrative long-term pact.

The plan worked, as Hernandez hit.272/.339/.501 with 33 homers over 652 plate appearances. He earned an All-Star nod, Silver Slugger honors, and (most importantly for Hernandez) his first championship ring as Los Angeles captured the 2024 World Series. As one might expect, Hernandez’s first choice was to remain in Dodger Blue, and that ended up being the case when L.A. re-signed him to a three-year, $66MM guarantee. The contract also carries a $15MM club option for 2028 ($6.5MM buyout), and a conditional $15MM club option for 2029 if Hernandez spends 75 days on the injured list due to a surgery for a specific injury.

The Dodgers won another World Series in 2025 with Hernandez putting up decent numbers during that postseason run. Overall, however, the first two years of Hernandez’s contract have looked a lot more like his 2023 than his 2024. Since Opening Day 2025, Hernandez has hit.256/.308/.441 with 41 homers over 1037 PA, translating to a 105 wRC+. The 2026 campaign saw Hernandez increase his batting average and walk rate from 2025 (though his 8.6BB% was still below league average), but his power diminished.

articles.title: Astros Hire Conner Watson As Director Of Hitting
body: The Astros have hired Conner Watson as their new director of hitting, The Athletic’s Chandler Rome reports. Watson heads to Houston after spending the last two seasons as the Guardians’ assistant director of hitting development.

The new hire continues an offseason of change for an Astros team that is looking for both a new GM and manager. In this case, Watson fills a role that has been open since August, when former director of hitting Dan Hennigan departed for a coaching job on the Wake Forest staff.

Spencer Medick was hired as Houston’s director of pitching earlier this week, so the Astros now have two division heads in place overseeing the entire organization’s pitching and hitting approaches. It is perhaps a little unusual that Medick and Watson were hired in advance of a general manager taking the wheel of baseball operations, though it perhaps tracks given how Astros owner Jim Crane is known for his active role in front office decisions.

Before joining the Guardians, Watson spent three years as a lead instructor at Driveline’s Arizona branch. He’ll now look to shake up and perhaps modernize the Astros’ hitting practices at both the major and minor league levels. While many of Houston’s coaches and manager Joe Espada won’t be returning in 2027, hitting coach Victor Rodriguez was expected to be retained, though this could potentially change depending on Watson’s plans.

articles.title: A Look At Jacob Latz’s Breakout Season
body: The Rangers’ bullpen was an underwhelming group in 2026. It combined for a 4.47 earned run average, 20.0% strikeout rate, 8.7% walk rate, and 39.2% ground ball rate. Only the walk rate was better than league average. Among the positives in the ‘pen was left-hander Jacob Latz. A veteran of parts of five big league seasons, he emerged this year as something of an unlikely closer.

The 30-year-old Latz held opponents to a sharp 2.13 ERA in 72 innings while earning 30 saves in 34 opportunities. The main change from prior seasons was a surge in strikeout rate. He previously sat in the 20-22% range but struck out 30.6% of opponents in 2026. Latz also brought his walk rate down by 2.1% to a roughly average 8.5%, which left his K-BB rate at 22.1%, good for 14th-best among 147 qualified relievers. ERA estimators were similarly kind, as Latz’s 2.65 xERA and 2.96 SIERA were both career-best marks in a full season.

Those expected numbers were significant improvements over 2025. In that season, Latz delivered a 2.84 ERA in 85 2/3 innings as a swingman, but his 4.11 xERA and 4.37 SIERA painted him as fairly lucky. He kept the ball in the yard, although his 21.8% strikeout rate and 10.6% walk rate were far from the levels he’d post in 2026. Before that, Latz had walked 14.1% of opponents in 43 2/3 innings in 2024. He only pitched 11 innings in the Majors from 2021-23 and spent all of 2022 at Triple-A Round Rock.

articles.title: Can Colson Montgomery Keep This Up?
body: The White Sox surprised the league by winning 84 games this year and earning a Wild Card spot in the playoffs. They ultimately fell to the Guardians in a five-game Division Series, but they’ll be looking to win the division next year on the back of a strong position player group. One member of that group is shortstop Colson Montgomery. Putting it simply, he had a polarizing season in 2026.

The 24-year-old Montgomery played in 153 games and took 638 trips to the plate. Among the positives, he led American League shortstops with 31 home runs, 87 runs batted in, and a.206 isolated slugging percentage. The power was clearly present, and it was a key reason for Montgomery being an everyday player despite only posting a 91 wRC+. His glovework also helped out significantly. Montgomery was worth +10 Outs Above Average at shortstop and ranked in the 94th percentile by Fielding Run Value, according to Statcast.

Altogether, Montgomery was worth 2.8 wins above replacement in the eyes of FanGraphs. That landed in the middle of the pack for qualified shortstops, and on the surface, it makes him a quality regular. However, Montgomery achieved that value while struggling badly to make contact. He batted.197/.282/.403 overall and struck out at a staggering 35.6% rate. The latter was the highest in the league not just among shortstops, but qualified players at any position. Montgomery’s teammate Munetaka Murakami came in second with a 35.4% strikeout rate.

body: The Dodgers fell short in their pursuit of a three-peat but the roster is still loaded with talent for another run in 2027.

articles.title: Austin Wells’ Impact On The Yankees’ Offseason
body: The Yankees were connected to pretty much every vaguely available catcher last season. The rumblings stemmed from a need to improve an Aaron Judge -less lineup, along with the struggles of the in-house options.

Austin Wells was the key figure in the catching discussions. His brutal first half led the club to entertain finding an upgrade. It didn’t help that there wasn’t a suitable backup. J.C. Escarra was demoted in June. Journeyman Ali Sanchez was little more than a stopgap.

Parsing Wells’ 2026 season will dictate how New York handles the catcher position this offseason. He entered the All-Star break with a.504 OPS. Wells bounced back in a big way over the final two months of the season, slashing.229/.343/.441 with seven homers. He stayed hot in the playoffs, going 5-for-15 with four RBI. Wells trying to stretch a double into a triple in the eighth inning of Game 1 of the ALDS grabbed the headlines. It’s easy to forget that his big swing broke up a no-hitter on a night Drew Rasmussen was virtually untouchable.
[Related: New York Yankees Offseason Outlook]

Of course, the tale of two seasons is much more complicated. Wells hit the injured list in early June with what were described as cervical headaches. The backstop took multiple foul tips to the mask early in the season, but passed concussion tests at the time. Persistent headaches eventually landed him on the IL. He returned after two weeks. Wells didn’t immediately get going at the plate, but he clearly performed better after the time off.

articles.title: Pablo Lopez On Track In Tommy John Recovery
body: Twins right-hander Pablo Lopez is working his way back from a February elbow procedure. He returned to playing catch in August and is targeting a return in Spring Training. His current outlook would make starting the year on the Opening Day roster a possibility.

Lopez didn’t need full Tommy John surgery. Instead, he had an internal brace procedure, which carries a shorter recovery timeline. A 12-month rehab process would put him back in a Twins uniform for spring action.
“In my case, chronologically speaking, I’m going to go straight into spring training, straight into the fire,” Lopez told Bobby Nightengale of the Minnesota Star Tribune.

The February surgery marked the second TJ for Lopez. His first go-round was all the way back in 2013, as a minor leaguer in Seattle’s system. That was a more standard recovery timeline, with the surgery coming at the end of the 2013 campaign and wiping out his 2014 season.

“I’m going to have to find ways to make sure that I’m listening to my body, make sure I’m keeping an eye on things that I didn’t have to experience with my first Tommy John because I was done with rehab, and I had a normal offseason where I had rest and recovered,” Lopez said.

The Lopez injury was part of a tumultuous winter for the Twins. The organization introduced new minority owners in December. Tom Pohlad took over as the team’s control person. Team president Derek Falvey departed in January. Then came the Lopez injury, followed by a Joe Ryan scare that ended up being just lower back inflammation.

articles.title: Guardians Notes: Kwan, Velazquez, Rotation
body: The Guardians won the American League Central for the third straight year and reached the doorstep of the World Series in 2026, but their season ended with a six-game loss to the Rays in the ALCS. With their championship hopes dashed again, Guardians president of baseball operations Chris Antonetti, general manager Mike Chernoff and assistant GM Matt Forman met with the media on Thursday to wrap up 2026 and discuss the upcoming offseason.
[RELATED: Guardians Offseason Outlook]

The Guardians aren’t at risk of losing outfielder Steven Kwan to free agency this winter, but the two-time All-Star only has one year of control left. MLBTR contributor Matt Swartz projects an $11.3MM salary for Kwan in his third and final trip through arbitration. That’s an eminently reasonable salary for a player of his caliber, though it’s a pricey figure for a team that had the lowest payroll in baseball (around $75MM). The Guardians have a history of trading away productive veterans with dwindling team control, evidenced by deals in which they shipped out Josh Naylor, Francisco Lindor, Corey Kluber, Carlos Carrasco, Trevor Bauer and Mike Clevinger. With that in mind, Kwan could be an offseason trade candidate. However, if we’re to believe Guardians brass, he isn’t going anywhere.
“As we sit here today, we’re expecting Steven Kwan to be a big part of a contending team next year,” Antonetti said (link via Paul Hoynes of cleveland.com).

articles.title: NL East Notes: Murphy, Mets, Marlins, Compton, Miller
body: Before Pat Murphy was promoted from bench coach to Brewers’ manager in November 2023, Murphy was known to be one of the finalists in the Mets’ 2019 managerial search that eventually resulted in the hiring of Carlos Beltran. Then-Mets GM Brodie Van Wagenen (who is now Murphy’s agent) preferred Murphy as the hire and made that recommendation to former COO Jeff Wilpon, as Van Wagenen and Murphy told the New York Post’s Joel Sherman.

Less than three months after being hired, Beltran resigned in January 2020 as part of the fallout from the Astros’ sign-stealing scandal. Murphy said the Mets reached out to him at the time and he was still interested in the managerial job, but the team ended up promoting from within by installing quality control coach Luis Rojas for the role. Van Wagenen said that decision was made with a nod to continuity, as Rojas was already a known quantity and Spring Training was just around the corner.

Needless to say, the Brewers are glad that Murphy stayed put, as the club is now three wins away from a World Series title with the skipper at the helm. It is anyone’s guess as to whether or not Murphy would’ve been able to similarly thrive in New York, but Milwaukee’s continued success under Murphy adds some salt to the Mets’ revolving door in the dugout. Counting Beltran, the Mets have had seven different managers within the last decade, and the hope that is interim-turned-permanent manager Andy Green can finally bring some stability.

articles.title: Todd Benzinger Passes Away
body: Former big leaguer Todd Benzinger passed away on Wednesday at age 63, according to a statement released by the Reds earlier this week. Three of Benzinger’s nine MLB seasons (from 1987-95) were spent in Cincinnati, with the switch-hitter playing a memorable role in the Reds’ World Series-winning squad in 1990.

A fourth-round pick for the Red Sox in the 1981 draft, Benzinger spent his first two Major League seasons with Boston before he was dealt to the Reds as part of a five-player swap in December 1988. It was a virtual homecoming for Benzinger, whose birthplace of Dayton, Kentucky is right across the Ohio River from Cincinnati. Benzinger made a bit of history in his very first at-bat as a Red, as his RBI single in the first inning on Opening Day 1989 officially ended Orel Hershiser’s regular-season scoreless-inning streak at a record 59 innings.

Acting as the Reds’ everyday first baseman in 1989, Benzinger moved into more of a platoon role the next season as both a first baseman and occasional left fielder. Benzinger did get the start at first in Game 4 of the 1990 World Series, and he’ll forever be remembered in Cincinnati for recording the final out (a Carney Lansford pop-up in foul territory) that sealed the Reds’ sweep of the Athletics.

“[Benzinger] was a super nice guy,” former Reds teammate and Hall-of-Famer Barry Larkin told MLB.com’s Mark Sheldon. “He was always a hard worker, not real loud. Just about doing his business. He was just a steady, consistent contributor. There was no craziness about him. He fit in well with the team. Just a really good, solid guy.”

articles.title: Yankees Extend Pitching Coach Matt Blake
body: TODAY: Blake and the Yankees have agreed to a new contract covering the 2027-29 seasons, according to Jon Heyman of the New York Post.
OCTOBER 23: The Yankees are expected to work out a new contract with pitching coach Matt Blake, reports Joel Sherman of the New York Post. His deal was set to expire at the end of the year.

Blake has been New York’s pitching coach since 2020. He’d been with the organization previously as a scout, before joining the Guardians as a minor league pitching coordinator in 2016. Blake was bumped up to assistant director of player development in 2017, a role he held through the 2019 season. His work in the Guardians system led to a big-league gig with the Yankees.

New York had to navigate several major injuries in the rotation this season. Gerrit Cole began the year on the IL as he recovered from elbow surgery. The same goes for Clarke Schmidt and Carlos Rodon. Max Fried dealt with elbow issues multiple times during the regular season. The club added Ryan Weathers in an offseason trade with the Marlins. The lefty helped stabilize the back of the rotation until Cole and Rodon returned. Weathers was lost to a flexor strain near the end of August.

articles.title: Yankees Notes: Boone, Judge, Massey
body: The Yankees made the decision to bring manager Aaron Boone back for a tenth season. Boone, who’ll become the seventh skipper in franchise history to reach a decade with the club, is under contract via the two-year extension he signed in February 2025.

Owner Hal Steinbrenner told reporters on Wednesday that there’d not yet been any conversations with Boone regarding another extension (link via Bryan Hoch of MLB.com). While that doesn’t necessarily mean they won’t discuss that at some point, Boone said that managing on an expiring deal “doesn’t bother (him) at all.” He pointed out that players and coaches frequently work without long-term contractual certainty, though many teams prefer not to have their managers or top front office executive in a lame duck capacity.

The Yankees allowed general manager Brian Cashman to hold his position on an expiring deal in 2026. The GM himself announced Wednesday that he and the team were finalizing an extension, one that’ll likely ensure that Cashman reaches three decades in the GM role. He’s already by far the longest-tenured active general manager, having ascended to the job in February 1998.

articles.title: Royals Outright Five Players
body: 9:01pm: Marsh indeed elected free agency as well, according to the tracker.

3:35pm: The Royals have sent five right-handed pitchers outright to Triple-A Omaha, according to the MLB.com transactions tracker. They are Alex Lange, Mason Black, Connor Seabold, Alec Marsh and Easton McGee. This indicates the club put the five of them on waivers recently and they all went unclaimed. Seabold and McGee have elected free agency. Marsh and Lange are also eligible to choose the open market and will presumably do so.

This part of the calendar is a big time for roster moves of this nature. After the World Series, eligible players become free agents but also the injured list goes away. Most teams have a handful of players on the 60-day IL who either need to be reinstated to the 40-man or bumped off. Players eligible for the Rule 5 draft also need roster spots in November if the club wants to protect them from selection. With all those moving parts, many fringe players will be squeezed off roster spots in the coming weeks.

Seabold, 31 in January, was acquired from the Blue Jays in a June trade. That didn’t work out for the Royals. Seabold allowed five earned runs in five innings before hitting the IL with a lat strain. He started a rehab assignment in September but was still on the IL at season’s end. He has a previous career outright, which gave him the right to elect free agency this time.

articles.title: MLBPA Withdrew Revenue Sharing Grievance Against Rays Last Year
body: The Major League Baseball Players Association withdrew its grievance against the Rays for not adequately spending revenue sharing money last December, according to a report from Ronald Blum of The Associated Press. The union filed the grievance against four low-payroll teams — the Rays, Marlins, Pirates and Athletics — way back in February 2018, as Marc Topkin of The Tampa Bay Times covered at the time. (Jeff Todd also wrote a contemporaneous post for MLBTR eight years ago.) The status of the grievances against the other teams is unclear.

Revenue sharing recipients are required by the collective bargaining agreement to spend that money to improve their on-field product. The CBA intentionally leaves the means very open-ended, however, so there’s no requirement it needs to be directly spent on player payroll. Spending on the front office, coaching, scouting, analytics, and player development all contribute to the on-field product and are appropriate means of using revenue sharing money.

It’s not clear precisely why the union withdrew the grievance against the Rays, though they evidently did so quietly nearly a year ago. However, it’s potentially not a coincidence that the decision came a few months after former owner Stu Sternberg finalized a sale of the franchise to Patrick Zalupski. The Rays subsequently garnered approval from Hillsborough County and the City of Tampa for a new stadium to open in 2029.

articles.title: Cardinals, Hitting Coach Brant Brown Part Ways
body: The Cardinals are moving on from hitting coach Brant Brown, as first reported by Katie Woo of The Athletic. Brown has been with the club for the past two seasons.

St. Louis ranked 16th in scoring this past season. The club finished in the bottom five in OPS, wOBA, and wRC+. The Cardinals were similarly underwhelming on offense in 2025, ranking in the bottom 10 in those three metrics.

Brown was hired heading into the 2025 campaign. He’s had several big-league stops along the way. After a decade coaching in the minors, Brown joined the Dodgers as an assistant hitting coach in 2018. He moved on to the Marlins in 2023 as their top hitting coach. Brown also had a brief stop in Seattle before coming to St. Louis.

Woo adds that the Cardinals are expected to keep the majority of manager Oli Marmol’s staff. Derrick Goold of the St. Louis Post-Dispatch reports that outfield coach Jon Jay and third base coach Ron Warner will be retained by the team for next season. Jay and Warner were both on expiring contracts.

While the offense as a whole came up short, there were several bright spots in 2026. The biggest development was the breakout of Jordan Walker. The former top prospect blasted 29 homers and stole 22 bases en route to his first All-Star selection. Walker made some batting stance tweaks that helped him get more out of his top-of-the-charts bat speed. He lowered his groundball rate and hit more homers in 2026 than he had from 2023 through 2025.

articles.title: Brewers, Rays Announce World Series Rosters
body: The World Series starts tonight with the Brewers hosting the Rays. The action kicks off at 7 pm CT. Both clubs have submitted their 26-man squads for the matchup.

The Brewers are rolling with 13 pitchers and 13 position players. The big news is Brandon Woodruff, who makes the final cut after a long layoff. The veteran righty had been working his way back from a shoulder injury and hoped to be ready for the Fall Classic. He hasn’t pitched in the majors since early July. Milwaukee expressed concern about being able to replace Woodruff on the roster if he made it and then had a setback. Apparently, those concerns have dissipated.

It’ll be Kyle Harrison and Shane Drohan filling out the back half of the pitching staff, with Woodruff taking Chad Patrick’s spot. Drohan tossed an inning against the Dodgers in the NLCS. Harrison and Patrick haven’t pitched at all. Antonio Senzatela has also been used sparingly, pitching twice in the NLDS and then not at all in the last round. The Brewers have leaned heavily on Trevor Megill, Abner Uribe, and Aaron Ashby, who have combined for 18 appearances. Ashby has covered 12 1/3 innings already, which ranks ninth among all pitchers this postseason.

The hitting group is unchanged for Milwaukee. Christian Yelich and Andrew Vaughn likely remain in a platoon at DH. The matchup against the Rays favors the lefty-swinging Yelich, given that Tampa Bay’s four-man rotation is entirely right-handed. Luis Lara and David Hamilton are on the bench as speed/defensive replacement options.

articles.title: Offseason Outlook: Cleveland Guardians
body: The Guardians again rode another strong September to their third straight AL Central title. They nabbed a first-round bye and overcame a 2-0 deficit to bounce the White Sox en route to the ALCS. Cleveland looked generally overmatched against the best team in the American League, though, and they again face questions about whether there’s enough offensive talent to truly rank among World Series contenders.

articles.title: Two Pitchers Elect Free Agency
body: Veteran right-handers Connor Brogdon and Carlos Hernández elected free agency earlier this week, according to the MiLB.com transactions log. Both hurlers had been with the Guardians organization.

The Guardians gave Brogdon a major league contract worth $900K last winter, but the low-cost flier didn’t pan out. The 31-year-old made 16 appearances out of the bullpen and pitched to a 5.06 ERA in 16 innings. Even though Brodgon walked just three hitters, allowing five home runs made it difficult to hold a spot on the Guardians’ roster. They outrighted Brogdon twice during the season, including in late September, and he could only muster a 6.35 ERA in 11 1/3 innings when he took the ball for Triple-A Columbus.

Cleveland was the fourth major league organization for Brogdon, whom the Phillies took in the 10th round of the 2017 draft. He debuted three years later and put together the best stretch of his career from 2021-22, a 101 2/3-inning run of 3.36 ERA pitching with solid strikeout and walk percentages of 23.6 and 6.9, respectively. Big league success has eluded Brogdon since then, though, as he has combined for a 5.59 ERA in 95 frames with the Phillies, Dodgers, Angels and Guardians dating back to 2024.

articles.title: Marlins Willing To Listen To Offers For Otto Lopez, Xavier Edwards
body: Teams inquired about Marlins shortstop Otto Lopez and second baseman Xavier Edwards before the Aug. 3 trade deadline, but the double-play tandem stayed put. Edwards and Lopez could continue their partnership in 2027, though the Marlins are willing to listen offers for both players if teams offer “a lot” in exchange, Barry Jackson of the Miami Herald reports.

Edwards and Lopez are each on track to make the first of three potential trips through arbitration this winter, meaning they are controllable through 2029. MLBTR contributor Matt Swartz projects a $5.4MM salary for Lopez and a $3.5MM payday for Edwards.

Lopez, whom the Marlins stole off waivers from the Giants in 2024, has combined for 10.7 fWAR since he landed in Miami. The 28-year-old was a below-average offensive player from 2024-25, but he slashed a career-best.305/.349/.437 with a 122 wRC+ in 687 plate appearances this season. Although Lopez didn’t hit for much power (11 home runs,.132 ISO) or draw many walks (5.8%), he fanned just 13% of the time. Consistently putting the ball in play helped the speedster to the majors’ fifth-highest batting average and seventh-most stolen bases (34).

Adding in Lopez’s well-regarded work at short, where he accounted for 14 Outs Above Average, 12 Fielding Run Value and 6 Defensive Runs Saved, he was among the majors’ most valuable players this year. Lopez tied Brewers second baseman Brice Turang for fifth in fWAR (5.9) and finished seventh in bWAR (6.1).

articles.title: Guardians’ Kahlil Watson Undergoes Core Muscle Surgery
body: The Guardians announced this week that outfielder Kahlil Watson underwent surgery Tuesday to repair a bilateral core muscle (sports hernia) injury. The team didn’t provide an exact timetable for his recovery but noted that similar cases tend to come with a timeframe of eight to 12 weeks for returning to play.

Watson, 23, will head into the 2027 season as a depth option in Cleveland. A first-round pick by the Marlins in 2021, he initially drew top prospect fanfare but saw his production wane early in his minor league tenure. Watson went from Miami to Cleveland as part of the 2023 trade swapping out the unwanted contracts of Jean Segura and Josh Bell. He spent parts four seasons in the Guardians’ system before making his major league debut this season.

The Guardians promoted Watson in mid-June and kept him on the big league roster into late May. He totaled 91 plate appearances but managed only a tepid.239/.264/.341 with a homer and nine steals (in 10 attempts). Watson fanned a whopping 32 times in that small sample and drew just three walks. He was more productive in Triple-A, where he batted.247/.361/.455 with 19 homers, 24 steals, a 13.3% walk rate and a 26.7% strikeout rate in 442 trips to the plate. He turned in comparable numbers at the Double-A and Triple-A levels in 2025.

articles.title: Manager Stephen Vogt Staying With Guardians
body: Although Guardians skipper Stephen Vogt has close ties to the state of Washington, he is not interested in the Mariners’ managerial vacancy. Vogt made it clear on Thursday that he is sticking with the Guardians.
“I’ll be in Cleveland,” Vogt told Tim Stebbins of MLB.com and other reporters. “I’m here. I’m coming back.”

Next season will be Vogt’s fourth in Cleveland, which won the American League Central in each of his first three years. After earning AL Manager of the Year honors from 2024-25, Vogt is a finalist again this fall. The former major league catcher guided the Guards to the ALCS for the second time in 2026, but the team is now in the early stages of the offseason after losing in six games to the Rays. While Cleveland took two of the first three, Tampa Bay then won three straight by a combined score of 17-7. It was a bitter ending for Cleveland, though it’s impressive that the club got that far after opening the season with a league-low payroll in the neighborhood of $75MM.

Teams in need of a manager would have coveted Vogt had he been a free agent this offseason, but he signed a multiyear extension after the 2025 campaign. While it’s unknown how many years are left on the contract, Guardians president of baseball operations Chris Antonetti told Zack Meisel of The Athletic he has “every expectation that Vogt is going to manage here for a really long time.”

articles.title: Red Sox, Riley Adams Agree To Minor League Deal
body: The Red Sox and catcher Riley Adams are in agreement on a minor league contract, reports Ari Alexander of 7News in Boston. The Ballengee Group client will presumably be in camp as a non-roster player next spring.

Adams, 30, spent the season in Triple-A with the Nationals, who removed him from their 40-man roster back in January. He hit.273/.389/.506 with 16 homers in 324 plate appearances (135 wRC+). Since the Nats didn’t add Adams to the 40-man roster and he has more than three years of major league service time, he was eligible to become a minor league free agent, which he did following the season.

A former third-round pick, Adams has played parts of five seasons in the majors, mostly with Washington. He has plenty of raw power but hasn’t gotten to it often in games at the big league level, where he’s a career.211/.287/.354 hitter with a 32.5% strikeout rate.

Defensively, Adams has repeatedly graded out as a poor framer but has turned in decent marks in terms of blocking balls in the dirt and throwing. He’s played a little first base in his career but has spent the overwhelming amount of his time at catcher and designated hitter. Adams has played parts of four seasons at the Triple-A level and posted a.260/.373/.489 batting line in 764 plate appearances there.

articles.title: Rangers Putting Sebastian Walcott Through Outfield Drills
body: Rangers top prospect Sebastian Walcott is currently getting extra at-bats in the Arizona Fall League. While he’s there, the club is having him work out in the outfield, per Evan Grant of the Dallas Morning News.

Walcott has only played shortstop and third base in the minors. He hasn’t played an AFL game in the outfield yet, but the club hopes to get him some reps on the grass. Director of player development Josh Bonifay has been running Walcott through outfield drills before games.

“I feel confident going into the outfield,” Walcott told Grant. “I just feel like it’s pretty simple. Like you’re just running balls down, catching fly balls. I feel it’s just pure athleticism out there in the outfield.”

The 20-year-old Walcott was in the mix for a big-league roster spot before an elbow injury wrecked his season. He had an internal brace procedure to address the issue and didn’t suit up until mid-July. Walcott had another strong minor league season, slashing.322/.398/.586 with nine home runs and 11 steals in just 37 games at Double-A. He played two games at Triple-A to finish the year.

Walcott will probably open the year at Triple-A, but he should be contributing with the Rangers soon enough. Adding the ability to play the outfield will only strengthen his bid for a promotion. Walcott is currently blocked at shortstop by Corey Seager. Josh Jung had a solid season as the everyday third baseman. There’s a vacancy at DH with Joc Pederson heading to free agency, but Texas might be hesitant to stunt Walcott’s defensive growth by sticking him there every day.

articles.title: Nationals To Keep Coaching Staff
body: The Nationals’ dugout will look the same in 2027. The club plans to bring back manager Blake Butera’s entire staff, reports Spencer Nusbaum of The Athletic.

Washington underwent a massive overhaul last offseason, starting with the installation of president of baseball operations Paul Toboni. The former Red Sox exec brought on Butera, a first-time manager. Both men were the youngest in the league in their respective roles.

The staff hired by Toboni and Butera also skewed heavily on the younger side. Pitching coach Simon Mathews (30), for example, was less than half the age of his predecessor, Jim Hickey (64). The three hitting coaches (Matt Borgschulte, Andrew Ayt, Sean O’Malley) were all in their early-to-mid 30s when hired.

The Nats won 77 games in 2026, their highest mark since 2019, when they won the World Series. It’s been a slog since winning the title, but the new regime offered hope this season. Washington headed into August just a game under.500 and with an outside chance of sticking in the NL Wild Card race. An 11-18 month ended any thoughts of a postseason bid. The team finished on a high note, winning 10 of its final 14 games.

While the coaches will remain in place, changes are expected to come on the training side. Nusbaum reports that the Nats declined to re-up with five members of the training staff. Director of medical services Harvey Sharman left in early September. The team also declined to renew the contracts of head strength and conditioning coach Brett Henry, head athletic trainer Dale Gilbert, and assistant trainers Jonathan Kotredes and Eric Montague.
